**Short answer:** This study alone isn't a good reason to stop. The "91%" figure comes from weak evidence. Since 16:8 is working for your weight, keeping it is reasonable. A slightly wider window, such as 10 hours, would also be reasonable if you'd rather be cautious.

**Where the number comes from**
- The "91% higher risk of cardiovascular death" was first presented as a conference abstract at an American Heart Association meeting in March 2024. It hadn't been peer-reviewed. ([NBC](https://www.nbcnews.com/health/heart-health/intermittent-fasting-risk-cardiovascular-death-rcna143853))
- The peer-reviewed version came out in 2025. It followed 19,831 US adults from a national nutrition survey for a median of about 8 years. People eating within less than 8 hours had a higher risk of cardiovascular death than those eating over 12–14 hours: HR 2.35, 95% CI 1.39–3.98. They had **no higher risk of death from any cause** or from cancer. The authors say confounding by other factors might explain the link. ([PubMed](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40849219/); [Medical Dialogues](https://medicaldialogues.in/amp/diet-nutrition/news/intermittent-fasting-under-8-hours-may-raise-heart-death-risk-by-135-percent-study-finds-153915))

**Why the evidence is weak**
- **Two days of data:** Eating windows came from just two 24-hour food recalls. Nobody was asked whether they were deliberately fasting, so the study wasn't really looking at people doing 16:8 for years. ([NBC](https://www.nbcnews.com/health/heart-health/intermittent-fasting-risk-cardiovascular-death-rcna143853))
- **Observational design:** It shows an association, not cause and effect. Short eating windows often go with skipped breakfasts, irregular work, smoking, illness or poor diet. Diet quality and calories weren't accounted for.
- **Imprecise estimate:** The confidence interval is wide, so the true effect could be anywhere in a large range. The headline figure also changed between the abstract and the paper (91% vs. 135%).
- **Caution from the author:** The lead researcher said it's too early to make recommendations from this study. ([NBC](https://www.nbcnews.com/health/heart-health/intermittent-fasting-risk-cardiovascular-death-rcna143853))

**What randomized trials show**
- Trials of time-restricted eating show modest weight loss and possibly lower systolic blood pressure, with no sign of harm to risk factors. ([meta-analysis](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC9644535/))
- In a 12-month trial, adding time restriction to calorie restriction gave no extra benefit. That suggests most of the benefit comes from eating less. ([NEJM trial](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35443107/))
- No trial has run long enough to measure deaths, so long-term safety is still unproven either way.

**Practical steps**
1. Get a yearly check of blood pressure, cholesterol (LDL) and blood sugar. Those numbers tell you more about your own risk than this study does.
2. Keep your diet quality high and eat enough protein. Add strength training, since one suggested explanation for the finding was lower muscle mass.
3. Tell your doctor about the regimen, especially if your health changes.

This is general information, not personal medical advice.

grade.decision_why: The answer matches the key's action. It says there is no strong reason to stop and calls continuing reasonable. It identifies the 91% figure as coming from one observational NHANES analysis first shown as a 2024 AHA abstract, and stresses association over causation and confounding. It notes that RCTs show no harm signal on risk markers. Telling a doctor is presented as optional general advice, not something the claim requires. It also adds accurate detail: the later peer-reviewed paper reported HR 2.35, and all-cause mortality was not raised.
rivals_in_answer: the association is confounded or reverse-caused (illness, diet quality, recall error)
a real small harm cannot be excluded by the data

# Why your dev container is slow on the Mac, and what to do

Two separate penalties multiply together. Your Linux colleagues pay neither of them.

**1. CPU emulation: Node and npm run as x86 code on an Arm chip.** Because of `--platform linux/amd64`, everything in the container is emulated, not just the one dependency. With QEMU, Docker says it "can be much slower" for CPU-heavy work like npm installs (https://docs.docker.com/build/building/multi-platform/). With Rosetta the penalty is smaller. Independent tests put it at roughly 20–36% (https://vpsmac.com/en/blog/docker-on-m4-mac-linux-container-performance-analysis.html, https://patrickwthomas.net/macos-docker/). Sources disagree on whether Rosetta is on by default (https://docs.docker.com/desktop/settings-and-maintenance/settings/ vs https://www.docker.com/blog/docker-desktop-4-25/), so check Settings yourself. Rosetta needs the Apple Virtualization framework VMM; Docker VMM doesn't support it (https://docs.docker.com/desktop/features/vmm/). Rosetta has also caused Node builds to hang or pin a CPU (https://github.com/docker/roadmap/issues/384, https://github.com/docker/for-mac/issues/7075). On macOS 27 there is an unconfirmed report that it got slower (https://github.com/orbstack/orbstack/issues/2744).

**2. The bind-mounted `node_modules`.** Every file operation on a bind mount crosses the VM boundary. In an independent benchmark, `npm install` took 9.5s on a bind mount and 3.6s with `node_modules` in a named volume (https://www.paolomainardi.com/posts/docker-performance-macos-2025/).

The two causes together (roughly 1.2–6× from emulation times about 2.8× from the mount) fit your 5–10×. Nobody has measured the exact split for this setup.

## What to do, in order

1. **Put `node_modules` in a named volume.** Keep the source bind-mounted and run `npm install` inside the container. VS Code documents the `devcontainer.json` mount for this (https://code.visualstudio.com/remote/advancedcontainers/improve-performance). This is cheap and the gain is reliable.
2. **Build the main image as native arm64.** Run the x86-only dependency as a separate amd64 service, or check whether an arm64 build of it now exists. This removes emulation from npm and the dev server entirely.
3. **If anything must stay amd64,** turn on Rosetta with the Apple Virtualization VMM. Turn it off again if you see hangs.
4. **Check file watching.** If `CHOKIDAR_USEPOLLING` or `WATCHPACK_POLLING` is set, polling a bind mount wastes CPU. Try without it under VirtioFS, but reports differ on whether native events work reliably (https://github.com/docker/for-mac/issues/7274).
5. **Optional:** Synchronized File Shares (paid plans) or OrbStack scored about the same as a named volume in Mainardi's test (https://docs.docker.com/desktop/features/synchronized-file-sharing/).

**To confirm the split,** time `npm ci` in four setups: amd64 vs arm64, each with and without the named volume.

grade.decision_why: The answer names both causes from the key: amd64 emulation on Apple Silicon and bind-mount overhead for node_modules. It gives the key's fixes for each: a named volume for node_modules, Synchronized File Shares or VirtioFS, a native arm64 image with the x86 dependency isolated, and Rosetta if amd64 must stay. It also proposes a four-way timing test that separates the two causes.
rivals_in_answer: amd64 emulation on Apple Silicon
bind-mount file sharing overhead (node_modules)
rivals_in_lanes: amd64 emulation on Apple Silicon
bind-mount file sharing overhead (node_modules)

Two separate problems are stacking up. Each one alone can cause a large slowdown on a Mac, but I haven't measured either on your setup.

**1. Your container runs x86 code on an ARM chip.** Because the image uses `--platform linux/amd64`, every Node and npm process is translated from x86 to ARM. Docker's setting "Use Rosetta for x86_64/amd64 emulation on Apple Silicon" is **off by default**, so it probably isn't using Apple's Rosetta translator. It most likely falls back to a slower emulator called QEMU. Docker says Rosetta makes x86 emulation "nearly on par with native", but that's Docker's own claim.

**2. node_modules sits on a bind mount.** On a Mac, Docker runs inside a small Linux virtual machine. Every file read or write in a bind mount has to cross between macOS and that VM. node_modules is tens of thousands of small files, so npm install and the dev server's file watching pay that cost constantly. Your Linux colleagues' containers read the disk directly, so they don't.

**What to do, in order of impact:**

1. **Move node_modules into a named volume.** Keep bind-mounting the source code, but add a volume on top: `- node_modules:/app/node_modules`. The files then live inside the VM. This also stops Linux-built packages from mixing with Mac ones on your disk.
2. **Turn on Rosetta.** In Settings, set the VM manager to Apple Virtualization framework, leave file sharing on VirtioFS (the default), and tick the Rosetta box. Run `softwareupdate --install-rosetta` first. One bug report says the box quietly unticks itself if Rosetta isn't installed.
3. **Stop running everything as x86.** Build a native ARM image and handle only the x86-only dependency on its own, for example in a separate amd64 sidecar container. Ask the vendor for an ARM build too. This matters beyond speed: Apple has said Rosetta is fully available only through macOS 27, which you're on now. Whether Docker's use of it continues in macOS 28 isn't confirmed.
4. **If it's still slow,** try Docker's synchronized file shares. They keep a cached copy of your files inside the VM. Add node_modules to `.syncignore`. Its documentation page doesn't say which Docker subscriptions include it.

Sources:
- https://docs.docker.com/desktop/settings-and-maintenance/settings/
- https://docs.docker.com/desktop/features/synchronized-file-sharing/
- https://www.docker.com/?p=47759
- https://github.com/docker/for-mac/issues/7243
- https://www.jeffgeerling.com/blog/2022/new-docker-mac-virtiofs-file-sync-4x-faster/
- https://engineered.at/articles/docker-on-macos-is-still-slow
- https://techearl.com/docker-bind-mounts-slow-mac-windows
- https://www.macrumors.com/2025/06/10/apple-to-phase-out-rosetta-2/
- https://developer.apple.com/forums/thread/787530

grade.decision_why: The answer names both live causes: amd64 emulation (QEMU by default, Rosetta off) and bind-mount overhead on node_modules. It gives the key's fixes for each: enable Rosetta or go native arm64 with only the x86-only piece isolated, and move node_modules to a named volume or use synchronized file shares on VirtioFS. It does not give a quick check that separates the two causes, such as timing npm install with node_modules in a volume versus on the bind mount, or arm64 versus amd64. It also ranks the fixes 'in order of impact' while admitting neither cause was measured.
rivals_in_answer: amd64 emulation on Apple Silicon
bind-mount file sharing overhead (node_modules)

**Short answer:** This study is not a good reason to stop. The evidence behind the "91%" claim is weak and doesn't really describe what you're doing.

**Where the number comes from**
- It was a March 2024 American Heart Association (AHA) conference poster that had not been peer-reviewed. It used US national survey data (NHANES) on about 20,000 adults.
- People who ate within less than 8 hours had a hazard ratio of 1.91 (95% CI 1.20–3.03) for cardiovascular death, compared with people eating over 12–16 hours. Death from any cause was **not** higher. The senior author said this does not show causation. https://www.heart.org/en/news/2024/03/18/time-restricted-eating-may-raise-cardiovascular-death-risk-in-the-long-term
- The peer-reviewed version (2025) compared against a 12–14 hour group and reported HR 2.35 (1.39–3.98). All-cause mortality was still not raised, and the authors flag possible residual confounding. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40849219/

**Why it's weak**
- **Eating window was measured badly.** It was inferred from two single-day food recalls. Nobody was asked whether they deliberately practised time-restricted eating (TRE), so a one-day snapshot stands in for your year-long 16:8 habit. Short recalled windows may also just be incomplete records.
- **Very small group.** In the poster, about 414 people (~2%) ate in under 8 hours, and 31 of them died. My researchers couldn't check the published paper's counts. https://www.tctmd.com/news/intermittent-fasting-study-sparks-debate-over-increases-cv-mortality
- **Confounding.** The short-window group smoked more and had more existing disease. Illness can also shorten eating windows. https://peterattiamd.com/time-restricted-eating-and-ascvd/
- **Expert pushback.** 34 researchers objected, and Yale's Krumholz called it "exploratory." https://fortune.com/well/2024/03/18/how-healthy-intermittent-fasting-heart-disease-study-91-percent-risk/

**Other evidence**
- A second NHANES analysis found the lowest risk at about 11–12 h. It uses the same data and the same flaw, so it isn't independent confirmation. https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/acel.70230
- A UK cohort found no link with mortality. https://www.nature.com/articles/s43856-025-01035-x
- Short trials show no harm to blood pressure or LDL cholesterol. They also show no benefit beyond weight loss, and none measured deaths. https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/nutrition/articles/10.3389/fnut.2025.1631477/full

**For you:** If 16:8 helps you control your weight, the weight control itself benefits your heart. This study gives no solid reason to drop it. It's also not proven to be better than ordinary calorie restriction (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37488260/), so a 10–12 hour window is a fine choice if you prefer it. A sensible step is to check your blood pressure, lipids and glucose with your doctor and decide based on those numbers.

**Decision: Don't run production on 3.13t.** For CPU-bound work, keep standard GIL 3.13 with multiprocessing. Ask the platform team to unpin 3.14 so you can pilot 3.14t. Don't ship 3.14t until that pilot passes on your own workload.

**Why 3.13t is ruled out**

- CPython calls 3.13t experimental. Its docs say to "expect some bugs" and a single-threaded slowdown of about 40%, and they list known ways to crash it. https://docs.python.org/3.13/howto/free-threading-python.html
- PEP 779 puts 3.13t in the experimental phase. Supported free-threading starts with 3.14t, where the single-thread cost drops to about 5–10%. https://peps.python.org/pep-0779/ and https://docs.python.org/3.14/whatsnew/3.14.html
- pypa/manylinux removed cp313t from its images on 2026-05-07, and PyTorch dropped 3.13t wheels as a result. https://dev-discuss.pytorch.org/t/dropping-python-3-13t-free-threaded-support-in-nightlies-and-in-the-future-pytorch-2-13-release/3386
- None of your three dependencies ships cp313t wheels in its current release. All three ship cp314t x86-64 wheels:
  - NumPy 2.5.4: https://pypi.org/project/numpy/#files
  - pydantic-core 2.50.4: https://pypi.org/project/pydantic-core/#files
  - lxml 6.1.3: https://pypi.org/project/lxml/#files
- Staying on 3.13t would mean building from source or pinning old releases. Old pins would miss security fixes, which matters most for lxml if it parses untrusted XML.
- If any extension isn't marked free-thread-safe, CPython turns the GIL back on for the whole process, which removes the benefit. https://pyo3.rs/v0.23.2/free-threading

**3.14t is promising but not proven for you**

- NumPy and pydantic both call their free-threading support experimental.
  - https://numpy.org/devdocs/reference/thread_safety.html
  - https://pydantic.dev/articles/pydantic-v2-11-release
- Writing to a shared NumPy array while another thread uses it can race, and resizing it can crash, so you would need your own locks.
- No one found an lxml statement on thread safety under free-threading. The lxml 7.0.0a1 notes call its support experimental. https://pypi.org/project/lxml/7.0.0a1/

```text
Decision: No 3.13t. Run GIL 3.13 with multiprocessing now, and pilot 3.14t after the platform pin changes.
Rests on: CPython's own docs and PEP 779 (3.13t is experimental); PyPI file lists checked by three researchers (no cp313t wheels for NumPy, pydantic-core or lxml; cp314t wheels for all three).
Not verified: whether your service on 3.14t actually runs with the GIL off, is faster than multiprocessing, and is stable with lxml and NumPy under threads.
Next check: On 3.14t, install your locked dependencies, start the service and assert sys._is_gil_enabled() is False. Then benchmark the real workload with 1 thread and N threads (throughput and memory) against GIL 3.14 with multiprocessing.
```

It makes that move conditional on checking cp314t wheels for all three dependencies and running a pilot on the real workload.

upgrade to 3.14+ and use its supported free-threaded build

No, not on 3.13t. Free-threading only becomes officially supported in 3.14t. If you want no-GIL in production, the path is to move your platform pin to 3.14.

**Why 3.13t is a bad bet**
- **Still experimental.** Python's own 3.13 docs say to "expect some bugs and a substantial single-threaded performance hit." That hit is about 40% on pyperformance, because 3.13t turns off the specializing interpreter. 3.13t also has known crash risks, such as sharing iterators or frame objects between threads, and some objects are kept in memory forever, which raises memory use. https://docs.python.org/3.13/howto/free-threading-python.html
- **Upstream has moved to 3.14t.** PEP 779 was accepted in June 2025 and dropped the "experimental" label for 3.14's free-threaded build, but it stays optional rather than the default. In 3.14 the single-threaded penalty is roughly 5–10%. https://peps.python.org/pep-0779/ · https://docs.python.org/3/whatsnew/3.14.html
- **The tooling is dropping 3.13t.** manylinux removed 3.13t from its build images on 7 May 2026, and PyTorch dropped 3.13t and told users to move to 3.14t. https://dev-discuss.pytorch.org/t/dropping-python-3-13t-free-threaded-support-in-nightlies-and-in-the-future-pytorch-2-13-release/3386
- **Your three dependencies have no current Linux x86-64 builds for 3.13t, but all have them for 3.14t:**
  - NumPy 2.5.4: https://pypi.org/project/numpy/#files
  - pydantic-core 2.50.4: https://pypi.org/project/pydantic-core/#files
  - lxml 6.1.3: https://pypi.org/project/lxml/#files

  pydantic-core did add 3.13t support back in 2.29.0 (https://newreleases.io/project/pypi/pydantic-core/release/2.29.0). Staying on 3.13t would freeze you on old versions or force you to build from source. If a package isn't marked as free-threading-safe, Python quietly turns the GIL back on with only a warning.

**What to do**
1. **Get 3.14t approved on your platform.** Without that, there's no supported no-GIL option for you.
2. **Benchmark your real workload on 3.14t** against normal 3.14, both with one thread and with many. Check `sys._is_gil_enabled()` at runtime and treat the GIL re-enable warning as an error in CI, so a single non-ready package can't silently switch the GIL back on.
3. **Audit your own thread safety.** The built-in list, dict and set types use internal locks, but Python doesn't guarantee that. Protect shared state with explicit locks, and don't share iterators, lxml trees or parsers between threads. I didn't find lxml documentation on how thread-safe it is under free-threading, so check that yourself.
4. **Run a canary rollout** that can fall back to the normal GIL build.
5. **Until 3.14t is approved,** run the CPU-bound work in a `ProcessPoolExecutor` on standard 3.13. Where it applies, NumPy code that releases the GIL already runs in parallel with plain threads.

Other source used: https://discuss.python.org/t/pep-779-criteria-for-supported-status-for-free-threaded-python/84319

answer.text:
**No, it isn't safe.** The SQLite docs rule out this setup: WAL mode doesn't work across machines, and even without WAL, SQLite on NFS is a known way to corrupt a database.

**Why WAL fails here**
- The WAL docs say: "All processes using a database must be on the same host computer; WAL does not work over a network filesystem." WAL keeps a "wal-index" in shared memory, made by memory-mapping a `-shm` file. "Processes on separate host machines obviously cannot share memory with each other." With three servers, each would have a different view of the WAL, which can lead to stale reads or corruption. https://www.sqlite.org/wal.html
- The only way to run WAL without shared memory is `locking_mode=EXCLUSIVE`, which allows a single process. That defeats the point of sharing the database.

**Why NFS is risky in any mode**
- SQLite depends on file locks and fsync ordering. "Some filesystems contain bugs in their locking logic… This is especially true of network filesystems and NFS in particular… database corruption might result." https://www.sqlite.org/howtocorrupt.html
- SQLite isn't tested over networks, and use over one is "at the user's risk… Rely upon it at your (and your customers') peril." https://www.sqlite.org/useovernet.html
- Rollback-journal mode reduces the risk but doesn't remove it. You also lose concurrent reads during writes, and every lock costs a network round trip.

**Load**
Twenty writes per second is easy for SQLite on a local disk. Over NFS, latency on each lock and sync makes contention and `SQLITE_BUSY` errors more likely. SQLite's guidance is to avoid it "where the same database will be accessed directly… and simultaneously from many computers over a network." It also says a site busy enough to need several servers should consider a client/server database. https://www.sqlite.org/whentouse.html

**What to do instead (best first)**
1. **Use PostgreSQL or MySQL.** This is the standard fix for several app servers sharing one database, and the SQLite docs recommend it.
2. **Run a single database owner.** Keep SQLite in WAL mode on local disk on one host, and have the other servers send requests to it through a small API or proxy. This is the pattern useovernet.html suggests. The trade-off is that the host becomes a single point of failure.
3. **Use a replicated SQLite system** such as rqlite, LiteFS or Turso/libSQL, if you want to stay with SQLite. I didn't research these within this budget, so check them yourself.

If you ignore this advice anyway, at least use rollback mode, not WAL, plus backups and regular `PRAGMA integrity_check` runs. Corruption is still possible.

Sources:
- https://www.sqlite.org/wal.html
- https://www.sqlite.org/useovernet.html
- https://www.sqlite.org/whentouse.html
- https://www.sqlite.org/howtocorrupt.html

grade.decision_why: The answer says no, which matches the key. It gives the key's reasons: SQLite's WAL docs say all processes must be on the same host with shared memory, and NFS locking is unreliable and risks corruption. It recommends the key's alternatives: a client-server DB, a single owner/writer service in front of SQLite, or a replication layer.

# Free-threaded Python for your service: not on 3.13t

**Short answer:** 3.13t is not production-ready for your stack. If free-threading matters to you, the real target is **3.14t**, and that means changing your platform's 3.13 pin.

## Why not 3.13t

- **Officially experimental.** CPython's own docs say to "expect some bugs and a substantial single-threaded performance hit." That hit is about 40% on pyperformance, because the specializing interpreter is turned off. The docs also list known crash cases, such as iterators shared between threads. Independent benchmarks put the penalty at 17–40%. https://docs.python.org/3.13/howto/free-threading-python.html, https://codspeed.io/blog/state-of-python-3-13-performance-free-threading
- **Support starts at 3.14.** PEP 779 makes 3.14t "officially supported but optional," with roughly a 5–10% single-thread cost. 3.13t stays experimental. https://peps.python.org/pep-0779/, https://docs.python.org/3.14/whatsnew/3.14.html
- **The ecosystem has dropped it.** manylinux removed cp313t on 2026-05-07, and PyTorch and others followed. https://dev-discuss.pytorch.org/t/dropping-python-3-13t-free-threaded-support-in-nightlies-and-in-the-future-pytorch-2-13-release/3386
- **Your dependencies have no cp313t wheels.** The current releases of NumPy 2.5.4, pydantic-core 2.50.4 and lxml 6.1.3 all ship cp314t wheels for manylinux x86-64, but none for cp313t. On 3.13t you would have to build from source or pin old, unmaintained versions. That is risky for lxml in particular, because it parses untrusted XML. https://pypi.org/project/numpy/#files, https://pypi.org/project/pydantic-core/#files, https://pypi.org/project/lxml/#files
- **One unready extension undoes the benefit.** Importing any extension that isn't marked free-thread-safe silently turns the GIL back on. https://pyo3.rs/v0.23.2/free-threading

## Caveats, even on 3.14t

- **Support is still labelled experimental.** NumPy, pydantic and lxml all describe their free-threading support that way. https://numpy.org/devdocs/reference/thread_safety.html, https://pydantic.dev/articles/pydantic-v2-11-release, https://pypi.org/project/lxml/7.0.0a1/
- **NumPy does no locking for you.** Writing to a shared array while another thread reads it is a race, and resizing it can crash the process, so you need your own locks.
- **lxml thread safety is unknown.** I found no official statement on sharing parsed trees across threads.

## What to do

1. **Now:** stay on the standard 3.13 build and use multiprocessing for the CPU-bound work.
2. **Ask the platform team to allow 3.14.** Then pilot 3.14t:
   - Leave `PYTHON_GIL` unset. Forcing `PYTHON_GIL=0` risks crashes.
   - At startup, assert that `sys._is_gil_enabled()` is False, and treat any GIL re-enable warning as a failure.
   - Benchmark your real workload single-threaded and at N threads against GIL-enabled 3.14. Measure memory as well as speed.
   - Stress-test shared NumPy arrays and lxml usage under heavy concurrency.
   - Check that your other dependencies support free-threading too.
3. **Keep a rollback path** to GIL-enabled 3.14 plus multiprocessing.

It also verifies cp314t wheels for each dependency and notes they are missing for cp313t.

**Decision: No, this study gives you no reason to stop your 16:8 routine.** The evidence behind the "91%" headline is weak, and it does not measure what you are doing.

**Where the number comes from**
- It was an unreviewed AHA conference poster from March 2024, based on about 20,000 US adults in NHANES. People eating within 8 hours had a hazard ratio of 1.91 (95% CI 1.20–3.03) for cardiovascular death. https://www.news-medical.net/news/20240318/8-hour-time-restricted-eating-schedule-may-increase-heart-disease-mortality.aspx
- The peer-reviewed version (*Diabetes & Metabolic Syndrome*, 2025) used a different comparison group and reported a hazard ratio of 2.35. All-cause and cancer deaths were not raised. The authors say the result may come from residual confounding. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40849219/

**Why it doesn't apply to you**
- **It didn't measure deliberate fasting.** Each person's "eating window" came from two single-day food recalls. Nobody was asked whether they practise time-restricted eating, so a year of planned 16:8 eating was never studied. https://www.tctmd.com/news/intermittent-fasting-study-sparks-debate-over-increases-cv-mortality
- **The group was tiny and different.** About 414 people (2% of the sample) ate within 8 hours, and 31 of them died of cardiovascular causes. That group smoked more, had more prior disease, and differed in other ways. Illness can also shorten eating windows rather than the other way round. https://peterattiamd.com/time-restricted-eating-and-ascvd/
- **Other cohorts don't confirm it.** A UK cohort found no link between eating window and mortality. https://www.nature.com/articles/s43856-025-01035-x A large French cohort linked a longer overnight fast to lower stroke risk. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10721609/ A second NHANES analysis that also flagged windows of 8 hours or less uses the same data and the same crude measure, so it is not independent support. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40944446/
- **Trials show no harm signal.** Randomised trials are short and only measure risk factors, not deaths. They find little change in blood pressure or LDL. https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/nutrition/articles/10.3389/fnut.2025.1631477/full
- **Experts dismissed it.** 34 researchers objected to the press release, and a past AHA president attributed the result to who the participants were, not when they ate (TCTMD link above).

**How strong is the evidence?** For harm to someone like you, it is weak: one observational dataset, a poor exposure measure, few deaths, and no all-cause effect. For benefit beyond weight loss, it is also weak. 16:8 is a reasonable weight-control tool, not proven heart protection.

**Not verified:** none of us could read the full 2025 paper, so its exact counts and adjustments are unchecked. They would not change this decision.

**Next check:** none needed.

I recommend citing that **about 19% of crates.io crates use the `unsafe` keyword directly** (Rust Foundation, May 2024). Present it as one of four independent measurements that all fall between **about 19% and 29%**. Quoting the range is more defensible than quoting 19.11% alone.

**Measurements by date**

| Study | Data | Direct `unsafe` | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Evans et al., ICSE 2020 (peer-reviewed) | about 15,000 crates that build | 29%; a further 38% have unsafe only through dependencies | [arXiv](https://arxiv.org/abs/2007.00752), [summary](https://alastairreid.github.io/RelatedWork/papers/evans:icse:2020) |
| Astrauskas et al., OOPSLA 2020 (peer-reviewed) | 31,867 crates | 23.6% | [OOPSLA page](https://2020.splashcon.org/details/splash-2020-oopsla/12/How-Do-Programmers-Use-Unsafe-Rust-); figure as cited in [this 2024 paper](https://arxiv.org/html/2404.02230v2) |
| Cui et al., arXiv preprint (not peer-reviewed) | 21,506 of 103,516 crates, snapshot 2023-01-30, regex search without compiling | 20.8% | [arXiv](https://arxiv.org/abs/2308.04785) |
| Rust Foundation blog | 24,362 of about 127,000 crates with "significant code", May 2024 | **19.11%**; 34.35% call into a crate that uses unsafe | [Rust Foundation](https://rustfoundation.org/media/unsafe-rust-in-the-wild-notes-on-the-current-state-of-unsafe-rust/) |

**How confident you can be**

- **High that it's roughly 1 in 5 to 1 in 4 crates.** Four studies with different methods and dates all land between about 19% and 29%.
- **Low on any exact decimal.** The 19.11% comes from a blog post, not a peer-reviewed paper. It doesn't define "significant code" or explain how it counted, and it's now 2.5 years old. I found no newer ecosystem-wide measurement.
- **The decline over time may not be real.** The figures fall from 29% to 19%, but the studies used different samples and methods, so the trend can't be read straight off them.
- **Direct use understates your exposure.** About 34–38% of crates reach unsafe code through their dependencies, and Evans found that more than half of crates aren't fully checked by the compiler. Popular crates use unsafe more: about 60% in Evans's sample of the most-downloaded crates. If your concern is your own dependency tree, the transitive figure matters more.
- **Using unsafe doesn't make code exploitable.** The Rust Foundation notes that most uses are calls into C/C++ libraries.

**For the auditors**

- I couldn't read the OOPSLA PDF itself. The 23.6% comes from the 2024 paper linked in the table, which attributes it to Astrauskas et al. Another summary I found [puts it at about 25%](https://alastairreid.github.io/RelatedWork/papers/astrauskas:oopsla:2020). Check the original ([DOI 10.1145/3428204](https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3428204)) before citing that row.
- The strongest evidence would be a scan of your own dependency tree with `cargo-geiger`.

# Unsafe code on crates.io: the figure to cite

**Cite: about 19% of crates.io crates directly contain `unsafe` code** (Rust Foundation, May 2024). Present it as "roughly one in five," not as a precise value. Confidence is moderate for the ~20% range and low for anything more exact.

## Main source

**Rust Foundation, "Unsafe Rust in the Wild," 21 May 2024.** It reports that 24,362 of about 127,000 crates "with significant code" use the `unsafe` keyword, stated as 19.11%. It also reports that 34.35% of crates make a direct call into a crate that uses `unsafe`.
https://rustfoundation.org/media/unsafe-rust-in-the-wild-notes-on-the-current-state-of-unsafe-rust/
The researchers also gave a `/news/` path for this post; check which URL resolves before publishing.

Auditors are likely to raise these points:
- **Undefined denominator.** "Significant code" is never defined, and about 18,000 of roughly 145,000 crates were excluded.
- **Arithmetic doesn't match.** 24,362 / 127,000 = 19.18%, not 19.11%, so the published denominator is rounded.
- **Not reproducible.** No dataset or method has been published, only the tool: https://github.com/rustfoundation/painter
- **Not peer-reviewed, and about 2.5 years old.** I found no census from 2025 or 2026.

## Independent check

**Cui, Sun, Xu & Zhou, ICSE 2024.** They found 21,506 of 103,516 crates using `unsafe` (snapshot 2023-01-30), which is about 20.8%. This was measured with a source-level scan, which is a different method from the Foundation's.
https://arxiv.org/abs/2308.04785
Another researcher found the same numbers in a later preprint by the same group (https://arxiv.org/html/2412.06251v1). Confirm the count appears in the ICSE version before citing it as peer-reviewed.

**Older context (2020):** Evans et al., ICSE 2020, report `unsafe` in "less than 30%" of libraries.
https://arxiv.org/abs/2007.00752

## Two warnings for a supply-chain assessment

1. **Direct use understates exposure.** About 34% of crates call directly into unsafe-using crates. Evans et al. found that more than half of libraries can't be fully checked by the compiler once dependencies are counted. Popular crates use `unsafe` much more often than the registry as a whole. State clearly whether your figure means direct use or dependency exposure.
2. **`unsafe` does not mean vulnerable.** Most uses are FFI (calls into C/C++) or SIMD, and the Foundation says so itself.

Don't cite the apparent decline from 29% to 19% as a trend. The studies use different methods and different sets of crates.

**Suggested wording:** "Approximately 19–21% of crates.io crates directly use `unsafe` (Rust Foundation, 2024; Cui et al., ICSE 2024). A larger share, over a third, depends directly on crates that do."

**Decision:** Two causes stack: the bind-mounted `node_modules` and amd64 emulation of all of Node. Fix the first now. For the second, run one timing test before restructuring the image.

**Do now (cheap, reversible):**
1. **Move `node_modules` into a named volume** and run `npm install` inside the container. Keep the source bind-mounted. In devcontainer.json, add `"mounts": ["source=${localWorkspaceFolderBasename}-node_modules,target=${containerWorkspaceFolder}/node_modules,type=volume"]` ([VS Code](https://code.visualstudio.com/remote/advancedcontainers/improve-performance)). An independent benchmark on Apple Silicon with Docker Desktop and VirtioFS measured `npm install` at 9.53s on a bind mount and 3.61s on a named volume, against 3.37s natively on the host ([Mainardi](https://www.paolomainardi.com/posts/docker-performance-macos-2025/)).
2. **Check Settings → General.** File sharing should be VirtioFS ([Docker settings](https://docs.docker.com/desktop/settings-and-maintenance/settings/)). Also look at what "Use Rosetta" is set to. The sources disagree on its default, so you need to see your own value.
3. **Remove `CHOKIDAR_USEPOLLING` / `WATCHPACK_POLLING`** if they are set. Polling a bind mount wastes CPU ([nuxt#27617](https://github.com/nuxt/nuxt.js/issues/27617)).

**Hold: switching to a native arm64 image.** Because of `--platform linux/amd64`, Node, npm and the dev server all run under emulation ([Docker multi-platform](https://docs.docker.com/build/building/multi-platform/)). Measured penalties range from about 1.2× to 6× ([patrickwthomas](https://patrickwthomas.net/macos-docker/), [VPSMAC](https://vpsmac.com/en/blog/docker-on-m4-mac-linux-container-performance-analysis.html), [orbstack#2744](https://github.com/orbstack/orbstack/issues/2744)). That spread is the difference between "not worth the refactor" and "the main problem." The fix would be an arm64 image, with the x86-only dependency in its own amd64 service. Turning Rosetta on is a fallback, but it has known hangs with Node ([roadmap#384](https://github.com/docker/roadmap/issues/384), [for-mac#7075](https://github.com/docker/for-mac/issues/7075)).

```text
Decision: named volume for node_modules + VirtioFS + no polling now;
          decide arm64 split after one timing test
Rests on: independent Apple Silicon benchmark (bind mount ~2.8× slower,
          volume ≈ native); emulation of the whole image follows from your
          --platform flag
Not verified: nothing was measured on your Mac; Rosetta vs QEMU on your
          machine; how much of your 5–10× comes from emulation
Next check: after step 1, time `npm ci` in your amd64 container and in a
          plain node:20 arm64 container (with the x86 dep removed), both
          with node_modules on a volume. A large gap means do the arm64
          split. Also check whether that dependency now ships arm64 binaries.
```

# No. It isn't safe as planned, and WAL makes it worse.

**WAL mode cannot work across hosts.** SQLite's documentation says: "All processes using a database must be on the same host computer; WAL does not work over a network filesystem." WAL keeps its index in a memory-mapped `-shm` file, and processes on three different servers can't share that memory. This is how WAL is designed, so mount tuning won't fix it. https://www.sqlite.org/wal.html

**NFS locking itself is a known source of corruption.** SQLite warns that fcntl locking "is broken on many NFS implementations" and that NFS locking bugs can corrupt the database. https://www.sqlite.org/faq.html (Q5), https://www.sqlite.org/howtocorrupt.html. The Linux NFS man page adds that NFS gives only close-to-open consistency, not cluster-level cache coherence. https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man5/nfs.5.html

**This has happened in production.** OpenAI's Codex docs report that WAL over shared NFS corrupted SQLite databases. Codex now detects NFS and forces rollback-journal mode. https://learn.chatgpt.com/codex/environments/network-file-systems (our researchers found this page at two slightly different paths). GoToSocial refuses to support SQLite on networked storage for the same reason. https://docs.gotosocial.org/en/latest/advanced/sqlite-networked-storage/

**Rollback-journal mode isn't a safe fallback.** It only allows many readers or one writer at a time. SQLite doesn't test it across a network, and its safety depends entirely on your NFS server getting locking right. Failures are "not frequent or repeatable," so passing tests prove little. https://www.sqlite.org/useovernet.html. Every lock also costs a network round trip. One report measured a 10–15x slowdown over NFS. https://sqlite.org/forum/forumpost/c04bf5be0e. Some people say they run SQLite on NFSv4 with "very few problems," but they don't report journal mode or how they check for corruption. https://sqlite.org/forum/forumpost/341635c1ffeb30fc?raw

**What to do instead**, in order of preference:

1. **Use PostgreSQL or MySQL.** SQLite itself recommends a client/server database for multi-server sites. https://www.sqlite.org/whentouse.html. 20 writes/s is trivial for either.
2. **Keep SQLite on one host's local disk** in WAL mode, and have the other two servers send reads and writes to it through a small service. SQLite endorses this setup. https://www.sqlite.org/useovernet.html
3. **Look at rqlite or LiteFS** if you want SQLite with replication. Our researchers didn't evaluate these, so check them yourself.

Whatever you choose, don't put the database on NFS with writers on three hosts.

grade.decision_why: The answer gives a clear 'No'. It cites SQLite's primary docs saying WAL does not work over a network filesystem and that NFS locking is unreliable and can corrupt data. It recommends a client/server database, a single host owning SQLite behind a service, or a replication layer (rqlite/LiteFS), which matches the key. One minor flaw: the 10–15x slowdown is cited to the wrong forum URL (c04bf5be0e instead of the Fossil post).

answer.text:
Probably not. The claim comes from one observational study with serious flaws, and it doesn't show that your 16:8 routine is dangerous.

**Where "91%" comes from**
- It was a March 2024 American Heart Association conference abstract based on US national survey data (NHANES), covering about 20,000 adults followed for a median of 8 years. People whose recorded eating fit in under 8 hours had a 91% higher rate of cardiovascular death than those eating over 12–16 hours. It was promoted with a press release before any peer review ([NBC](https://www.nbcnews.com/health/heart-health/intermittent-fasting-risk-cardiovascular-death-rcna143853), [Smithsonian](https://www.smithsonianmag.com/smart-news/intermittent-fasting-linked-to-higher-risk-of-death-from-heart-disease-preliminary-study-finds-180983993/)).
- A version was published in 2025 in *Diabetes & Metabolic Syndrome*. It reports a hazard ratio of 2.35 for cardiovascular death and no link to death from all causes or cancer ([Medical Dialogues](https://medicaldialogues.in/diet-nutrition/news/intermittent-fasting-under-8-hours-may-raise-heart-death-risk-by-135-percent-study-finds-153915)).

**Why the evidence is weak**
- **It doesn't measure fasting habits.** Eating windows came from just two days of food recall, which were assumed to hold for years. A short window on two days isn't a deliberate, consistent routine like yours.
- **The group was small.** About 2% of participants were in it (roughly 414 people), so a chance result is more likely.
- **The groups weren't comparable.** The short-window group had about 60% more smokers, and sleep, shift work and diet quality weren't properly accounted for.
- The lead author says the study shows a link, not that eating windows cause heart deaths. 34 researchers in the field publicly criticized how it was promoted ([expert letter](https://blog.mycircadianclock.org/?p=13102), [Becker's](https://www.beckershospitalreview.com/cardiology/experts-cast-doubt-on-link-between-intermittent-fasting-heart-disease)).
- Another analysis of the same survey data found the lowest death risk at 11–12 hours of eating per day ([News-Medical](https://www.news-medical.net/news/20250915/Daily-meal-timing-influences-longevity-risk-in-adults-study-reveals.aspx)). These datasets give conflicting signals.

**What trials show**
- Randomized trials find time-restricted eating safe in the short term, with weight loss about equal to ordinary calorie cutting ([2025 meta-analysis](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12479299/)).
- Long-term outcomes like heart attacks and deaths haven't been tested. Researchers raise possible concerns about muscle loss and late eating ([Frontiers 2025](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/nutrition/articles/10.3389/fnut.2025.1524125/full)).

**What this means for you**
- If 16:8 keeps your weight under control, this study isn't a good reason to stop. It's a low-quality warning sign, not proof of harm.
- To be careful:
  - Eat earlier in the day rather than late.
  - Get enough protein and do strength training to protect muscle.
  - Eat good-quality food and don't smoke.
  - Check your blood pressure, lipids and glucose with your doctor.
- Your weight control matters more than the exact window. Widening to 10 hours would cost you little if that helps you worry less.

This is general information, not medical advice.

It reports no harm signal in randomized trials and calls checking with a doctor reasonable, not required. This matches the key's decision.

a real small harm cannot be excluded by the data

- Cui et al. include 3,614 yanked crates. Excluding them gives about 21.5%.

Rests on: Two independent whole-registry measurements of crates.io, agreeing within 2 points
Not verified: Nothing that would change the decision. No count newer than May 2024 exists.
Next check: None needed. Before submitting, open the Foundation URL below; one researcher reached it at /news/ instead of /media/.

# Should you stop 16:8 over the "91% higher heart death" headline?

**Short answer:** No, not on the strength of this evidence. It is a weak observational signal, not a demonstrated risk. It is still a reasonable prompt to check that 16:8 is actually helping you.

## Where the 91% comes from

The figure comes from a 2024 American Heart Association conference poster. It was not peer-reviewed at the time. The study used NHANES, a US survey of about 20,000 adults followed for a median of 8 years.

- People eating within a window of **under 8 hours** had HR 1.91 (95% CI 1.20–3.03) for cardiovascular death, compared with a 12–16 hour window.
- There was no link with all-cause or cancer death.
- The senior author said the study does not show that time-restricted eating caused the deaths.

https://newsroom.heart.org/news/8-hour-time-restricted-eating-linked-to-a-91-higher-risk-of-cardiovascular-death

A peer-reviewed version appeared in 2025 (Chen et al., *Diabetes & Metabolic Syndrome*), reporting HR 2.35 against a 12–14 hour window. I'm relying on secondary coverage for that figure: https://medicaldialogues.in/diet-nutrition/news/intermittent-fasting-under-8-hours-may-raise-heart-death-risk-by-135-percent-study-finds-153915

## Why the evidence is weak

- **Small group:** only 414 people (about 2%) were in the short-window group, with 31 cardiovascular deaths. https://www.tctmd.com/news/intermittent-fasting-study-sparks-debate-over-increases-cv-mortality
- **Thin measurement:** eating windows came from two days of food recall, then were assumed to hold for years.
- **Confounding:** the short-window group had more smokers and higher BMI.
- **Reverse causation:** illness or poverty can make people eat less. That is not the same as choosing 16:8.
- **Expert pushback:** a former AHA president called the result "not ready for prime-time," and 34 researchers objected to the press release. Spiegelhalter said it shouldn't have been publicised. https://www.sciencemediacentre.org/expert-reaction-to-conference-abstract-about-time-restricted-eating-and-cardiovascular-death/

A second NHANES analysis found a U-shaped curve, with the lowest risk at 11–12 hours. Its cardiovascular signal was mainly in older adults and was not significant in younger adults after full adjustment. It uses the same data and has the same flaws. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40944446/

No randomized trial has measured deaths, so a small real harm can't be fully ruled out.

## What's worth doing instead

- **Check it's working.** In one 16:8 trial, weight loss was no better than control, and much of the weight lost was muscle. Eat enough protein and do resistance training. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32986097/
- **Get routine checks** of blood pressure and lipids. Trials show modest effects of time-restricted eating on risk factors, not on outcomes. https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/nutrition/articles/10.3389/fnut.2025.1631477/full
- **Consider a gentler window** of around 10–12 hours if it suits you as well. Shorter isn't proven better.

It does not say outright that the trials show no cardiovascular harm signal, but the recommended action is the same.

You have two problems that make each other worse. Every process in the container, including `node` and `npm` themselves, runs as emulated x86 code. And all of the many small file operations in `node_modules` go through the slow Mac-to-Linux file sharing layer. Your Linux colleagues have neither problem: they run natively and their bind mounts are plain local disk access.

**1. Emulated amd64 (`--platform linux/amd64`)**
- An Apple Silicon Mac can't run x86 binaries directly. Docker Desktop translates them with QEMU, or with Rosetta, which is faster. Docker says Rosetta gives "near-native" speed, but that's a vendor claim. Independent users report native arm64 images are still much faster.
- Docker's settings page says the Rosetta option is off by default. Docker's 4.25 announcement says it's on by default on macOS 14.1+. Check it yourself: Settings → General → "Use Rosetta for x86_64/amd64 emulation on Apple Silicon". This needs the Apple Virtualization framework VMM. Docker VMM doesn't support Rosetta, so amd64 emulation there "is slow".
- **Best fix:** build the image as native arm64 and emulate only the one x86 dependency. First check whether it now ships arm64 builds. If not, you could run it as a separate amd64 service or install just that binary.

**2. `node_modules` on a bind mount**
- Bind-mounted files stay on the macOS side and cross into the Linux VM for every file operation. Named volumes live inside the VM and are much faster. npm install and file watching on tens of thousands of files is close to the worst case for this.
- **Fix:** keep the source code bind-mounted, but put `node_modules` in a named volume, e.g. `- node_modules:/app/node_modules` in Compose.
- Make sure file sharing is set to VirtioFS (the documented default) and not gRPC FUSE.
- For large repos, Docker Desktop's "Synchronized file shares" keeps a synced copy of the files inside the VM. Its docs give no benchmarks, and I couldn't confirm from the docs which paid plans include it.
- An alternative runtime, OrbStack, says its bind mounts are faster. That's the vendor's own benchmark.

**Order to try:** confirm Rosetta is on, move `node_modules` to a named volume, then work toward a native arm64 image. Together these should close most of the gap. I haven't measured that myself.

**Sources**
- https://docs.docker.com/desktop/settings-and-maintenance/settings/
- https://www.docker.com/blog/docker-desktop-4-25/
- https://docs.docker.com/desktop/features/vmm/
- https://docs.docker.com/desktop/features/synchronized-file-sharing/
- https://oneuptime.com/blog/post/2026-01-16-docker-mac-apple-silicon/view
- https://blog.nashcom.de/nashcomblog.nsf/dx/tips-running-domino-container-images-on-apple-silicon.htm
- https://orbstack.dev/blog/fast-filesystem
- https://techearl.com/docker-bind-mounts-slow-mac-windows

**Not on 3.13t.** If you want to try free-threading in production, the realistic route is CPython 3.14t, and lxml is the dependency that will hold you back.

**Why 3.13t is a dead end**
- PEP 779 calls the 3.13 free-threaded build "explicitly experimental" (Phase I). 3.14 is the first release where it's "officially supported but still optional": https://peps.python.org/pep-0779/
- The ecosystem has moved off 3.13t. manylinux removed 3.13t from its build images on 7 May 2026, and PyTorch dropped it for that reason: https://dev-discuss.pytorch.org/t/dropping-python-3-13t-free-threaded-support-in-nightlies-and-in-the-future-pytorch-2-13-release/3386
- On Linux x86-64, the current releases of your dependencies publish free-threaded wheels for 3.14t but not 3.13t:
  - NumPy 2.5.4: cp314t and cp315t only. https://pypi.org/pypi/numpy/2.5.4/json
  - pydantic-core 2.50.4: has cp314t, and I found no cp313t wheel. https://pypi.org/pypi/pydantic-core/2.50.4/json
  - lxml 6.1.3: has cp314t, and I found no cp313t wheel. https://pypi.org/pypi/lxml/6.1.3/json

  On 3.13t you'd have to pin old releases or build from source. Both are bad ideas in production.

**Dependency status on 3.14t**
- **NumPy:** has supported free-threading since 2.1 (https://py-free-threading.github.io/tracking/). Low risk.
- **pydantic:** support was added as experimental in 2.11. The free-threaded test suite became required in 2.13, and race conditions were still being fixed in 2.14.0b2 (Sept 2026): https://pypi.org/project/pydantic/. Usable, but test hard.
- **lxml:** this is the weak point. The changelog adds "Experimental support for freethreading Python… in 3.14t and later" only in **7.0.0a1**, which is an alpha: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/lxml/lxml/master/CHANGES.txt. The stable 6.1.3 cp314t wheels most likely turn the GIL back on when imported, which would remove the speedup. I haven't confirmed that.

**Costs to expect**
Single-threaded code runs about 8% slower on x86-64 Linux, and memory use goes up: https://docs.python.org/3.14/howto/free-threading-python.html

**What to do**
1. Don't ship 3.13t. Ask your platform team to allow 3.14 / 3.14t.
2. Build a 3.14t staging image. At startup, check `sys._is_gil_enabled()` and fail if it returns True, because any extension that lacks support quietly re-enables the GIL.
3. Benchmark it against **multiprocessing / ProcessPoolExecutor on regular 3.13**, which already uses all your cores with no ecosystem risk. That stays my default recommendation until lxml 7.0 is final.
4. Stress-test with many threads sharing objects. Avoid sharing iterators or mutable state across threads without locks.
5. If lxml stays experimental, keep XML parsing in a separate process or worker pool. Wait for lxml 7.0 final before using it in the free-threaded path.

**No, this isn't safe. The WAL part of your plan won't work at all.**

**1. WAL doesn't work across machines.** WAL mode keeps a shared-memory index in an mmapped `-shm` file. Every process that uses the database has to share that memory. The SQLite docs say: "All processes using a database must be on the same host computer; WAL does not work over a network filesystem… processes on separate host machines obviously cannot share memory with each other." Three servers on an NFS mount can't share that memory, so you risk corruption, not just slow performance.
https://www.sqlite.org/wal.html

**2. NFS locking itself is a corruption risk.** Even without WAL, SQLite relies on file locks to coordinate writers. The docs say locking bugs are "especially true of network filesystems and NFS in particular," and that "database corruption might result." They also say "there is nothing SQLite can do to prevent it." Your tests may pass and still miss the problem. SQLite isn't tested over a network, so this setup is "at the user's risk."
https://www.sqlite.org/howtocorrupt.html
https://www.sqlite.org/whentouse.html
https://www.sqlite.org/useovernet.html

**3. Even "working" rollback mode is a poor fit.** The SQLite docs list rollback-journal mode over the network as a way to reduce the risk. In that mode, writers block readers, and NFS delay makes each lock last longer. At 20 writes/sec across three hosts you'd likely see `SQLITE_BUSY` contention, and you'd still depend on NFS locks behaving correctly. Their rule of thumb is to avoid SQLite when the same database is "accessed directly… and simultaneously from many computers over a network."
https://www.sqlite.org/whentouse.html

**What to do instead** (the SQLite docs suggest the first two):
- **Use a client/server database.** The docs name PostgreSQL as "an excellent choice." For three app servers writing at the same time, this is my recommendation.
- **Keep SQLite on one machine behind a service.** Put the database in WAL mode on a single host's local disk. Have only processes on that host touch the file, and send the other servers' reads and writes to them over the network, through a small API or proxy. At 20 writes/sec, one SQLite writer can easily keep up.
- Replicated SQLite systems such as rqlite or LiteFS also exist. I didn't research them here, so check them yourself before relying on them.

Sources:
- https://www.sqlite.org/wal.html
- https://www.sqlite.org/useovernet.html
- https://www.sqlite.org/howtocorrupt.html
- https://www.sqlite.org/whentouse.html

grade.decision_why: The answer says no. It cites SQLite's WAL doc saying all processes must share memory on one host, so WAL does not work over a network filesystem. It flags NFS locking as a corruption risk and recommends a client/server database or a single-host SQLite service. It also mentions replication layers (rqlite/LiteFS) with a caveat. This matches the key's decision and alternatives.

# No, 3.13t isn't production-ready for this stack

Two things rule it out:

- **CPython calls 3.13t experimental.** The docs say to "expect some bugs and a substantial single-threaded performance hit." That hit is about 40% on pyperformance, though independent workloads measured 6–20%. 3.13t also never frees classes, modules, functions or code objects once a second thread starts, so memory grows. https://docs.python.org/3.13/howto/free-threading-python.html, https://static-frame.readthedocs.io/en/latest/articles/freethread.html, https://codspeed.io/blog/state-of-python-3-13-performance-free-threading
- **The ecosystem has dropped 3.13t.** manylinux removed it from its build images on 2026-05-07, and PyTorch followed. https://dev-discuss.pytorch.org/t/dropping-python-3-13t-free-threaded-support-in-nightlies-and-in-the-future-pytorch-2-13-release/3386
  - None of your dependencies' current releases ships cp313t wheels: NumPy 2.5.4, pydantic-core 2.50.4 and lxml 6.1.3. All three ship cp314t wheels. https://pypi.org/project/numpy/#files, https://pypi.org/project/pydantic-core/#files, https://pypi.org/project/lxml/#files
  - Staying on 3.13t would mean pinning old releases that get no security fixes, or building from source.

3.14 is the supported free-threaded target under PEP 779, with about 8% overhead on Linux x86-64. https://peps.python.org/pep-0779/, https://docs.python.org/3/howto/free-threading-python.html

**lxml is a risk even on 3.14t.** One researcher reports that lxml 6.x turns the GIL back on when imported. Proper free-threading support appears only in 7.0.0a1, an experimental alpha. https://bugs.launchpad.net/lxml/+bug/2111289, https://pypi.org/project/lxml/7.0.0a1/

NumPy (2.1+) and pydantic-core (2.29+) are listed as supporting free-threading. That means they don't crash; it doesn't mean shared objects are safe to write from several threads without your own locks. https://py-free-threading.github.io/tracking/

## What to do

1. **Keep production on standard 3.13 for now.** If you need CPU parallelism today, a process pool (`multiprocessing` / `ProcessPoolExecutor`) is the low-risk route.
2. **Ask the platform team to allow 3.14t** and run a pilot there.
3. **Check the GIL at startup.** After all imports, assert `sys._is_gil_enabled()` is `False`. If lxml re-enables it, you lose the whole gain without any error.
4. **Contain lxml** until 7.0 is final: keep its calls on one thread, behind a lock, or in a worker process. Don't force `PYTHON_GIL=0` around it.
5. **Benchmark your own workload** against the GIL build, both single-threaded and multi-threaded, before switching.

## Caveats

- The PyPI file lists were only partly read, so a stray cp313t wheel can't be fully ruled out.
- The lxml GIL behaviour is reported by one researcher; step 3 will confirm it either way.
- No published production case studies of 3.13t were found.

It checks free-threaded wheels on 3.14 for all three dependencies (cp314t present) and flags lxml's re-enabling of the GIL as a remaining risk.

Lane 2 flagged that it was not confirmed from manylinux's own changelog, but the final answer states it as established and dropped that caveat.

upgrade to 3.14+ and use its supported free-threaded build

**No, this headline gives you no reason to stop.** The evidence behind it is weak: one observational signal that can't show cause, and it was measured in people who are not like you.

**Where "91%" comes from**
- It started as a 2024 American Heart Association conference poster, released before peer review. The study used about 20,000 US adults from the NHANES survey. Those eating within a window under 8 hours had a hazard ratio of 1.91 (95% CI 1.20–3.03) for cardiovascular death. There was no link with all-cause or cancer death. https://newsroom.heart.org/news/8-hour-time-restricted-eating-linked-to-a-91-higher-risk-of-cardiovascular-death
- Only 414 people (2%) were in that group, and 31 of them died of cardiovascular causes. The group had more smokers and higher BMI. https://www.tctmd.com/news/intermittent-fasting-study-sparks-debate-over-increases-cv-mortality
- Eating windows came from just two days of food recall. Nobody asked whether people ate that way on purpose. A short window often meant illness, poverty or skipped meals, not a planned 16:8 like yours.
- The senior author said it "does not mean" that time-restricted eating caused the deaths. Experts, including a past AHA president and 34 researchers, criticised the press release. https://www.sciencemediacentre.org/expert-reaction-to-conference-abstract-about-time-restricted-eating-and-cardiovascular-death/
- A later peer-reviewed version reported HR 2.35, with the same design limits. https://medicaldialogues.in/diet-nutrition/news/intermittent-fasting-under-8-hours-may-raise-heart-death-risk-by-135-percent-study-finds-153915
- A second analysis of the same dataset found a U-shaped curve. It was not significant in younger adults after full adjustment. https://news-medical.net/news/20250915/Daily-meal-timing-influences-longevity-risk-in-adults-study-reveals.aspx
- Randomized trials show neutral-to-modestly-favourable effects on risk factors. https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/nutrition/articles/10.3389/fnut.2025.1631477/full

**Separate from the headline:** in one 16:8 trial, much of the weight lost was muscle. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32986097/ Whether 16:8 is still worth it for your weight is your call on its own merits.

Rests on: Authors and independent experts agree the study cannot show cause.

Next check: none needed

**Cite about 19% (roughly 1 in 5) of crates on crates.io that contain significant code use the `unsafe` keyword directly.** Source: Rust Foundation, "Unsafe Rust in the Wild," May 2024. The post says: "Of those 127,000 crates, 24,362 make use of the `unsafe` keyword, which is 19.11% of all crates." It also reports that **34.35% call directly into another crate that uses `unsafe`**. For supply-chain risk, that second number may matter more.
https://rustfoundation.org/media/unsafe-rust-in-the-wild-notes-on-the-current-state-of-unsafe-rust/

## Confidence

**High confidence in "about 20–25%". Low confidence in any decimal.** Independent studies using different methods land close together:

| Source | Snapshot | Crates | Share with unsafe |
|---|---|---|---|
| Rust Foundation (Painter tool) | May 2024 | ~127,000 | 19.11% |
| Cui et al., Fudan (arXiv 2412.06251) | 2023-01-30 | 103,516 | 21,506 crates, which I calculate as ≈20.8% |
| Astrauskas et al., OOPSLA 2020 | ~2020 | 31,000+ | ~25% (75% use none) |
| Evans et al., ICSE 2020 | ~2019 | ~15,000 | 29% ("less than 30%" in the abstract) |

https://arxiv.org/html/2412.06251v2 · https://arxiv.org/abs/2007.00752v1 · https://alastairreid.github.io/RelatedWork/papers/astrauskas:oopsla:2020 · https://alastairreid.github.io/RelatedWork/papers/evans:icse:2020

## Caveats to disclose

- **No peer review.** The Rust Foundation figure is from a blog post. It doesn't define "significant code" or publish Painter's method.
- **Small arithmetic gap.** 24,362 ÷ 127,000 = 19.18%, not 19.11%. The 127,000 is probably rounded, so cite "≈19%".
- **The data is old.** It's from May 2024, about 2.5 years ago, and the registry has grown since. I found no newer measurement of this metric.
- **Different definitions.** The studies count different things: the keyword itself, unsafe blocks, or unsafe functions. Don't present them as a time series.
- **Popular crates are higher.** Evans found over 50% among the most-downloaded crates.
- **Don't confuse with advisory failures.** A January 2026 blog post reports 24.2% of crates failing cargo-deny's "unsound" advisory check. That measures known advisories, not unsafe usage (https://mr-leshiy-blog.web.app/blog/crates_io_analysis/).

I couldn't extract text from the Evans or Astrauskas PDFs, so those rows come from the arXiv abstract and secondary summaries. Before auditors check them, confirm both against the primary papers (Astrauskas: https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3428204).

## Two causes stack, and Linux laptops have neither

**1. Everything runs under x86 emulation.** `--platform linux/amd64` emulates all of Node, npm and your build tools, not only the one dependency. Rosetta is much faster than QEMU, but it is only available with the Apple Virtualization framework VMM. The sources disagree on whether it is on by default. Docker's current settings page lists it as "Disabled" ([settings](https://docs.docker.com/desktop/settings-and-maintenance/settings/)), while the 4.25 announcement says it is enabled on macOS 14.1+ ([4.25 post](https://www.docker.com/blog/docker-desktop-4-25/)). On "default settings" you may be running on QEMU, which is far slower ([Docker multi-platform docs](https://docs.docker.com/build/building/multi-platform/)). Rosetta also has known problems: no AVX, hangs, and 100% CPU ([roadmap #384](https://github.com/docker/roadmap/issues/384)). npm install on node:20 under emulation has a specific hang bug ([docker-node #1946](https://github.com/nodejs/docker-node/issues/1946)).

**2. `node_modules` on a bind mount.** Each file operation crosses the macOS-to-VM sharing layer (VirtioFS). npm install and file watching do huge amounts of small-file I/O, which is the worst case for that layer. GOV.UK measured a compile dropping from about 19s to about 4s after moving `node_modules` to a named volume ([GOV.UK ADR](https://docs.publishing.service.gov.uk/repos/govuk-docker/adr/0003-use-docker-volumes-for-improved-macos-performance.html)). Other reports put npm install at roughly 3.5× slower on a bind mount ([benchmark](https://eastondev.com/blog/en/posts/dev/20251217-docker-mount-comparison/)).

No source splits your 5–10× between the two causes. A plausible estimate is about 3–5× from the mount, with the rest from emulation.

## What to do, in order

1. **Today:** In Settings > General, select the Apple Virtualization framework and turn on Rosetta.
2. **Today:** Mount a named volume over `node_modules` and keep the source bind-mounted ([VS Code guide](https://code.visualstudio.com/remote/advancedcontainers/improve-performance)). The cost is that the IDE can't see `node_modules` on the host. "Clone Repository in Container Volume" goes further.
3. **Measure:** Time `npm ci` with the mount vs the volume, and with Rosetta on vs off. This shows which cause dominates for you.
4. **Real fix:** Build the image native arm64 and isolate the x86-only dependency. Check for an arm64 release first, and if there isn't one, run it in an amd64 sidecar. Apple is phasing out Rosetta after macOS 27 ([MacRumors](https://www.macrumors.com/2025/06/10/apple-to-phase-out-rosetta-2/)), so an amd64-only setup is a long-term risk.
5. **Upgrade off Node 20.** It reached end-of-life on 2026-04-30.
6. **If it's still slow:** Try Synchronized File Shares, which needs a paid plan ([docs](https://docs.docker.com/desktop/features/synchronized-file-sharing/)), or OrbStack. OrbStack's speed claims are vendor-only ([OrbStack](https://orbstack.dev/blog/fast-filesystem)).

grade.decision_why: The answer names both key causes, amd64 emulation and node_modules on a bind mount, and says they stack. It gives a fix for each: Apple Virtualization framework plus Rosetta, a native arm64 image with the x86 dependency isolated, a named volume for node_modules, and Synchronized File Shares as a fallback. It also includes the separating check the key asks for: a 2x2 timing of npm ci (mount vs volume, Rosetta on vs off).
grade.E3_evidence: "Apple is phasing out Rosetta after macOS 27 ([MacRumors](...)), so an amd64-only setup is a long-term risk." This rests only on news coverage and is applied to Rosetta-for-Linux in Docker as settled, although the lane report flagged that it is unclear whether Rosetta for Linux VMs is affected. Also, "npm install on node:20 under emulation has a specific hang bug" is stated as established when its only source is an issue tracker that was closed without a confirmed root cause.
rivals_in_answer: amd64 emulation on Apple Silicon
bind-mount file sharing overhead (node_modules)

bind-mount file sharing overhead (node_modules)

**Figure to cite:** About **1 in 5 crates (19.11%)** use the `unsafe` keyword directly. This is 24,362 of the roughly 127,000 crates the Rust Foundation classed as having "significant code," as of May 2024.
https://rustfoundation.org/news/unsafe-rust-in-the-wild-notes-on-the-current-state-of-unsafe-rust/

Always state the denominator. The post calls this a share "of all crates," but against all ~145,000 crates it would be about 16.8%. The 19.11% only works against the "significant code" subset, and the post never defines that term. Auditors will probably notice this.

**Corroborating sources (same order of magnitude):**
- **Cui et al. (2023 snapshot):** 21,506 of 103,516 crates, about 20.8%, found by regex matching. https://arxiv.org/html/2412.06251
- **Astrauskas et al., OOPSLA 2020:** about 31,867 crates. Roughly 20% have unsafe blocks and about 13% declare unsafe functions. A later survey gives the total as 23.6%. https://doi.org/10.1145/3428204 · survey: https://arxiv.org/html/2404.02230v3
- **Evans et al., ICSE 2020:** the abstract says "less than 30%." The 29% figure appears only in secondary sources. https://arxiv.org/abs/2007.00752

Together these show the share falling slowly, from about 29% in 2016–2018 to about 19–21% in 2023–24.

**Transitive exposure:** This is often the more relevant figure for supply-chain risk. 34.35% of crates directly call a crate that uses `unsafe` (same Rust Foundation post). Evans et al. report that "more than half" have `unsafe` somewhere in their call chain.

**Confidence:**
- **High** that roughly 1 in 5 crates use `unsafe` directly.
- **Low** on the exact decimal. The Foundation's method (its Painter tool, https://github.com/rustfoundation/painter) is thinly documented, has not been peer reviewed, and has not been independently replicated.
- No measurement from 2025 or 2026 exists, so the figure is about 2.5 years old.

**Caveats to state in the assessment:**
- Studies define "unsafe" differently: the keyword anywhere, unsafe blocks, unsafe function declarations, or regex hits.
- Containing `unsafe` does not make a crate vulnerable. Much of it is calls into C/C++ code.
- Do not cite the 23.6% figure as Astrauskas's own number; it comes from the later survey. None of the researchers read the full Evans or Astrauskas papers.

**Recommendation:** Cite 19.11% with its denominator and date, and give the 19–24% range as corroboration. For the strongest audit trail, also run `cargo-geiger` on your own dependency tree. Your actual exposure is a figure you can reproduce, which matters more than the ecosystem average.

# No, this setup isn't safe. WAL mode across hosts is the main problem.

## Why

1. **WAL can't work across machines.** WAL coordinates through a shared-memory index, the `-shm` file, which each process memory-maps. Three servers can't share memory over NFS, so each one would see a different index. SQLite's docs say: "All processes using a database must be on the same host computer; WAL does not work over a network filesystem." NFSv4's better locking doesn't change this, because the issue isn't locking. https://www.sqlite.org/wal.html
2. **NFS locking is a known cause of corruption.** SQLite singles out "network filesystems and NFS in particular." Its FAQ says to avoid NFS when several processes access the file at once. https://www.sqlite.org/howtocorrupt.html, https://www.sqlite.org/faq.html
3. **"It worked in testing" proves little.** SQLite says network failures are rare and hard to reproduce, and it doesn't test network setups. Richard Hipp, SQLite's author, told one user whose cross-host WAL test passed: "that just means you didn't test it enough." https://www.sqlite.org/useovernet.html, https://mail-archive.com/sqlite-users@mailinglists.sqlite.org/msg108685.html
4. **People have hit this exact failure.** OpenAI's Codex docs report corruption when Linux hosts share a WAL database over NFS. GoToSocial doesn't support NFS at all, with or without WAL. Nextcloud users on NetApp NFS reported corruption on every restart. https://learn.chatgpt.com/codex/environments/network-file-systems (one researcher cited a slightly different path for this page), https://docs.gotosocial.org/en/latest/advanced/sqlite-networked-storage/, https://help.nextcloud.com/t/storage-over-nfs-on-netapp-corrupts-database/41506

Rollback-journal mode is less risky, but it's still unsupported. Every write would also block all readers across the network, which at 20 writes/s means latency and `SQLITE_BUSY` errors.

## What to do instead

Your load of 20 writes/s is easy for SQLite on a single host. The problem is the three-server layout, not the volume. Pick one of these:

- **PostgreSQL or MySQL.** This is SQLite's own advice for sites that need several servers. https://www.sqlite.org/whentouse.html
- **One server owns the SQLite file** in WAL mode on local disk. The other two servers send reads and writes to it through an API. https://www.sqlite.org/useovernet.html
- **A replication layer** such as LiteFS or rqlite. We didn't evaluate these.

## Also

SQLite's corruption page describes a "WAL-reset" race that can corrupt a database even on a single host. One researcher reported that it affects versions 3.7.0 through 3.51.2. Check your SQLite version against https://www.sqlite.org/howtocorrupt.html whichever option you choose.

grade.decision_why: The answer gives a clear No. It grounds that in SQLite's primary docs: WAL requires a single host with shared memory, and NFS locking is unreliable and risks corruption. It recommends the same alternatives as the key: a client-server DB, a single owning host with an API or proxy in front, or a replication layer.

**Short answer:** No. For a healthy 45-year-old, this headline isn't a good reason to stop. The evidence behind it is weak.

**Where the claim comes from**
- It started as a March 2024 conference abstract presented at an American Heart Association (AHA) meeting, not a peer-reviewed paper. The study used US national survey data (NHANES, 2003–2018) for about 20,000 adults, linked to death records, with a median follow-up of 8 years. People who ate within an 8-hour window had a "91% higher" risk of cardiovascular death (HR 1.91) than people who ate over 12–16 hours. They did not have higher risk of death from all causes or from cancer.
- The full paper came out in August 2025 in *Diabetes & Metabolic Syndrome*. It reported HR 2.35 for an eating window under 8 hours compared with 12–14 hours. The authors themselves point to "residual confounding," meaning other differences between the groups may explain the result.

**Why the evidence is weak**
- **It shows a link, not a cause.** It can't show that the eating window caused the deaths.
- **Eating habits were measured from only two days.** Each person's window came from two 24-hour food recalls, which were then assumed to describe their eating over many years. Nobody in the study was actually following a planned 16:8 diet.
- **The numbers are small.** Only about 414 people (2%) were in the short-window group, and 31 of them died of cardiovascular causes. The 95% confidence interval runs from 1.20 to 3.03, so the true effect could be much smaller.
- **The groups differed from the start.** The short-window group had more smokers and higher body weight. Experts suggested that some people ate in short windows because of shift work or hardship, not by choice. Cardiologist Donald Lloyd-Jones said the result was "not ready for prime-time." Another expert, Pam Taub, said 34 researchers objected to how the AHA publicized it.

**The other side of the evidence**
Short randomized trials of time-restricted eating show modest improvements in weight, insulin, blood pressure and cholesterol, and few side effects. One 2025 meta-analysis found no loss of lean muscle. No trial has measured long-term heart deaths either way.

**What to do**
- If 16:8 is working for you, it's reasonable to continue.
- Focus on what you eat as well as when: plenty of protein, regular strength training to protect muscle (low muscle mass was one possible explanation the researchers raised), and no smoking.
- Get blood pressure, lipids and glucose checked as usual for your age.
- Stop and talk to a doctor if you get dizziness or palpitations, notice signs of disordered eating, or start a medication such as a diabetes drug.

**Sources**
- https://www.tctmd.com/news/intermittent-fasting-study-sparks-debate-over-increases-cv-mortality
- https://www.heart.org/en/news/2024/03/18/time-restricted-eating-may-raise-cardiovascular-death-risk-in-the-long-term
- https://medicaldialogues.in/diet-nutrition/news/intermittent-fasting-under-8-hours-may-raise-heart-death-risk-by-135-percent-study-finds-153915
- https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/nutrition/articles/10.3389/fnut.2025.1664412/full

grade.decision_why: Like the key, the answer says there is no strong reason to stop and that the evidence is weak. It traces the 91% figure to one NHANES observational analysis first shown as a 2024 AHA conference abstract. It calls the finding an association with confounding, small subgroups and recall limits, and notes that trials show no harm on risk markers. It suggests seeing a doctor only for specific symptoms or medication changes, which fits the key's 'reasonable but not required'.
rivals_in_answer: the association is confounded or reverse-caused (illness, diet quality, recall error)
a real small harm cannot be excluded by the data
