**Decision:** Cite **"about one in five crates on crates.io (19.11%) use the `unsafe` keyword directly"** (Rust Foundation, May 2024). Back it with the independent 2023 count of **20.8%** from Cui et al. Confidence is high that the figure is about one in five for direct use as of 2023–24. Present it as "about 19%" rather than leaning on the decimals.

**Rests on:** Two independent full-registry measurements of crates.io that were read in their primary text and agree:
- **Rust Foundation, "Unsafe Rust in the Wild" (21 May 2024):** 24,362 of about 127,000 crates "with significant code" use `unsafe`, measured with its Painter tool. https://rustfoundation.org/news/unsafe-rust-in-the-wild-notes-on-the-current-state-of-unsafe-rust/
- **Cui et al., arXiv:2412.06251 (snapshot 30 Jan 2023):** 21,506 of 103,516 crates contain unsafe code, about 20.8%, counted by matching patterns in the source. https://arxiv.org/html/2412.06251

Older counts were higher, which fits a share that has been falling. Ozdemir found 1,048 of 3,638 crates (about 29%) in 2016: https://cs.stanford.edu/~aozdemir/blog/unsafe-rust-syntax/. The Evans et al. ICSE 2020 abstract says "less than 30%": https://arxiv.org/abs/2007.00752

**Tell the auditors this up front:**
- The Foundation post calls 19.11% the share "of all crates." The arithmetic only works if the base is the roughly 127,000 crates "with significant code," a term the post never defines. Measured against all 145,000 crates, the share would be about 16.8%.
- The definitions differ between sources: the Foundation counts the `unsafe` keyword, while Cui counts pattern matches in the source.
- For supply-chain risk, exposure through dependencies is larger. The Foundation says 34.35% of crates call directly into a crate that uses `unsafe`, and the Evans abstract says "more than half" have unsafe code somewhere in their call chain.

**Do not cite:**
- "23.6%" and "29%/29.4%": no researcher found these in a primary text.
- The Astrauskas OOPSLA 2020 percentages: these came only from a secondary summary.

**Not verified:** No count from 2025 or 2026 was found, so the figure is current only to May 2024. Date-stamp it ("as of May 2024"). That keeps it defensible and doesn't change what to cite.

**Next check:** None needed for the crates.io figure. If the assessment also needs your *own* exposure, run `cargo-geiger` on your dependency tree. That measures a different thing from this figure; it is not a precondition for citing it.

**Decision:** Don't put the SQLite database on the NFS mount with all three servers writing to it. Use one of these instead:

- **PostgreSQL or MySQL.** This is the simplest fit for three app servers. At about 20 writes/s, load isn't a concern for either.
- **One server owns the SQLite file** on its local disk, in WAL mode. The other two servers send their reads and writes to it through an API.

**Rests on:** WAL mode depends on a shared-memory index (the mmapped `-shm` file). Processes on different machines cannot share that memory, so the three servers would each see a different index. This is a design limit, not a tuning issue, and NFSv4's improved locking doesn't change it.

- SQLite's documentation says: "All processes using a database must be on the same host computer; WAL does not work over a network filesystem." https://www.sqlite.org/wal.html
- SQLite's author says that cross-host WAL tests which appear to pass mean "you didn't test it enough." https://mail-archive.com/sqlite-users@mailinglists.sqlite.org/msg108685.html
- OpenAI's Codex docs report this failure in practice: Linux hosts sharing a WAL database over NFS corrupted it. https://learn.chatgpt.com/codex/environments/network-file-systems (one researcher cited it at …/docs/environments/network-file-systems)

Turning WAL off doesn't make it safe either:

- SQLite names NFS locking as a known cause of corruption. https://www.sqlite.org/howtocorrupt.html and https://www.sqlite.org/faq.html (Q5)
- SQLite says it is "not tested in across-a-network scenarios." Its own recommendation is a client/server database, or WAL on one host behind a proxy. https://www.sqlite.org/useovernet.html
- Its guidance for a site busy enough to need several servers is to use a client/server database. https://www.sqlite.org/whentouse.html
- Other projects say the same and report corruption: GoToSocial calls NFS unsupported with or without WAL (https://docs.gotosocial.org/en/latest/advanced/sqlite-networked-storage/), and a Nextcloud user saw corruption on NetApp NFS (https://help.nextcloud.com/t/storage-over-nfs-on-netapp-corrupts-database/41506).

**Not verified:** Nobody tested your own NFS server or mount options. That wouldn't change the decision, because the WAL limit applies to every NFS setup. No source supports rollback-journal mode over NFSv4 at your load either.

**Next check:** None needed for the decision. If you go with the single-owner option, it may be worth a short look at LiteFS or rqlite, which are built for replicating SQLite. None of the researchers evaluated them.

grade.decision_why: The answer commits to 'No' and recommends the same actions as the key: a client/server database (PostgreSQL/MySQL) or a single host owning the SQLite file behind an API. It also points to replication tools (LiteFS/rqlite) as an option. It grounds the decision in SQLite's primary documentation: WAL needs shared memory on one host, and NFS locking is unreliable.

## Short answer

Two separate slowdowns stack on top of each other, and both come from your Mac setup.

1. **Every binary in the container runs under x86 emulation.** With `--platform linux/amd64`, Node, npm and any native addons are all Intel code. Docker Desktop uses QEMU to run that code unless you turn on Rosetta, and Rosetta is **disabled by default**. Your colleagues' Linux laptops run the same image natively. ([Docker settings docs](https://docs.docker.com/desktop/settings-and-maintenance/settings/))
2. **`node_modules` is on a bind mount.** On a Mac, Docker runs inside a Linux VM, so every file operation on a bind mount crosses from the VM to macOS. The default VirtioFS is faster than the older options, but it's still much slower than a native filesystem. `npm install` writes tens of thousands of small files and the dev server watches them, so this is the worst case for that boundary. One user saw a Next.js compile take 25.5 s on a Mac versus 3.1 s on Ubuntu. ([OrbStack explainer](https://orbstack.dev/blog/fast-filesystem), [Docker forum](https://forums.docker.com/t/virtiofs-is-not-enabled-by-default-as-per-documentation-cannot-be-enabled-on-the-ux-and-fails-if-enabled-manually/145791))

## What to do, in order of payoff

1. **Put `node_modules` in a named volume** and bind-mount only your source code. In Compose that's `- .:/app` plus `- node_modules:/app/node_modules`, then run `npm install` inside the container. GOV.UK's team cut a build from about 31 s to about 4 s with this kind of change. One downside: your editor on the Mac won't see `node_modules`. ([GOV.UK ADR](https://docs.publishing.service.gov.uk/repos/govuk-docker/adr/0003-use-docker-volumes-for-improved-macos-performance.html), [engineered.at](https://engineered.at/articles/docker-on-macos-is-slow-and-how-to-fix-it))
2. **Turn on Rosetta:** Settings → General → "Use Rosetta for x86_64/amd64 emulation on Apple Silicon". This needs the Apple Virtualization framework VMM. ([Docker docs](https://docs.docker.com/desktop/settings-and-maintenance/settings/), [Atomic Object](https://spin.atomicobject.com/docker-apple-silicon/))
3. **Better long-term fix: stop emulating everything.** Build the image for arm64 and isolate only the x86-only dependency, for example in a small amd64 sidecar container. Also ask the vendor whether an arm64 build exists. This matters more over time: Apple says general-purpose Rosetta is available only through macOS 27. It hasn't confirmed whether the Linux-VM version that Docker uses survives past that, and Parallels expects it to go. ([MacRumors](https://www.macrumors.com/2025/06/10/apple-to-phase-out-rosetta-2/), [Parallels KB](https://kb.parallels.com/en/129871))
4. **If the source bind mount is still slow**, try Docker's **Synchronized file shares**. It keeps a synced copy of your files inside the VM and is aimed at large repos. Check whether your Docker subscription includes it. ([Docker docs](https://docs.docker.com/desktop/features/synchronized-file-sharing/))
5. Give Docker Desktop more CPU and memory, and keep VirtioFS selected as the file-sharing implementation.

Steps 1 and 2 together should remove most of the 5–10× gap. Some overhead will remain because Docker on a Mac always runs inside a VM.

grade.decision_why: The answer names both causes from the key: amd64 emulation (QEMU by default, Rosetta off) and bind-mount overhead that is worst for node_modules. It gives the key's fixes for each: a named volume for node_modules, Rosetta, a native arm64 image with only the x86 part isolated, synchronized file shares, and VirtioFS. One gap is that it has no quick diagnostic to tell the two causes apart, which the key lists as ideal but not required.
rivals_in_answer: amd64 emulation on Apple Silicon
bind-mount file sharing overhead (node_modules)

**Short answer:** No, not on 3.13t. Free-threading is officially supported only from **3.14t**, and none of your three dependencies currently ship 3.13t wheels. The real decision is whether your platform will move to 3.14.

**Why 3.13t is a dead end**
- PEP 703 was accepted for 3.13 explicitly as experimental. PEP 779, accepted June 2025, made the free-threaded build officially supported (still optional) only from 3.14. https://peps.python.org/pep-0779/ · https://discuss.python.org/t/pep-779-criteria-for-supported-status-for-free-threaded-python/84319
- manylinux removed 3.13t from its images on 7 May 2026, calling 3.14t "the stable, non-experimental free-threaded variant." PyTorch dropped 3.13t as a result. https://dev-discuss.pytorch.org/t/dropping-python-3-13t-free-threaded-support-in-nightlies-and-in-the-future-pytorch-2-13-release/3386

**Your dependencies (checked on PyPI today)**
- **NumPy 2.5.4:** has cp314t manylinux x86-64 wheels, no cp313t. https://pypi.org/project/numpy/#files
- **pydantic-core 2.50.4:** has cp314t, no cp313t in the current release. It first added 3.13t support in 2.29. https://pypi.org/project/pydantic-core/#files · https://py-free-threading.github.io/tracking/
- **lxml:** this is the blocker. The stable 6.1.3 has cp314t wheels, but its changelog never mentions free-threading. Real support ("Experimental support for freethreading Python… 3.14t and later") arrives only in **7.0.0a1**, an alpha. My guess, which I haven't confirmed, is that 6.x turns the GIL back on when it's imported. https://pypi.org/project/lxml/#files · https://lxml.de/changes-7.0.0a1.html

If an extension that isn't marked thread-safe gets imported, CPython quietly turns the GIL back on and only prints a warning. You'd pay the single-threaded cost (about 8% on x86-64 Linux) and gain nothing. https://docs.python.org/3.14/howto/free-threading-python.html

**What to do**
1. Stay on regular 3.13 in production. If you need CPU parallelism now, use `multiprocessing` or `ProcessPoolExecutor`, or move the hot loops into NumPy, which releases the GIL.
2. Ask your platform team for a 3.14 or 3.14t path. 3.13t won't get there.
3. Set up a 3.14t staging lane with NumPy, pydantic, and lxml 7.0 pre-releases. Check `sys._is_gil_enabled()` at startup and fail if it returns True. Run your test suite and benchmarks with many threads.
4. Go to production only after lxml 7.0 final is out and your benchmarks show the speedup outweighs the single-threaded cost and the higher memory use (PEP 779 cites about 15–20%).

grade.decision_why: The answer says no to 3.13t because it is experimental under PEP 703 and supported only from 3.14 under PEP 779. It recommends staying on the GIL build with multiprocessing or ProcessPoolExecutor, and planning a 3.14t move once free-threaded wheels for every dependency are confirmed (it waits on lxml 7.0 final). This matches the key's decision and action.
grade.E3_evidence: "manylinux removed 3.13t from its images on 7 May 2026, calling 3.14t 'the stable, non-experimental free-threaded variant.' PyTorch dropped 3.13t as a result." The only support is a PyTorch dev-discuss forum post retelling the manylinux change, yet it is stated as fact and used to call 3.13t 'a dead end'.
rivals_in_answer: stay on the GIL build and use processes
upgrade to 3.14+ and use its supported free-threaded build

# 28 April 2025 Iberian blackout: established cause and open disputes

**Caveat:** None of us could read the ENTSO-E final report itself, because the PDF was too large to fetch. The details in point 1 come from press summaries. Check each one against the report before you cite it in the brief.

## Established by official investigations

1. **ENTSO-E Expert Panel final report (20 Mar 2026).** There was no single root cause. Several factors interacted to cause "fast voltage increases and cascading generation disconnections":
   - two oscillations (about 0.6 Hz forced, and 0.2 Hz inter-area)
   - insufficient voltage and reactive-power control
   - renewables running at a fixed power factor
   - some protection tripping below the regulatory thresholds
   
   Iberia lost synchronism at 12:33:19. The panel describes this as Europe's first overvoltage blackout. Its chair said: "The problem is not renewable energy, but voltage control."
   - https://www.entsoe.eu/news/2026/03/20/entso-e-publishes-expert-panel-final-report-on-28-april-2025-blackout-in-spain-and-portugal/
   - https://www.entsoe.eu/publications/blackout/28-april-2025-iberian-blackout/
   - https://www.powermag.com/anatomy-of-a-blackout-findings-from-the-spain-portugal-grid-collapse-final-report/

2. **Spanish Government committee (17 Jun 2025).** It found the cause multifactorial. It blamed both Red Eléctrica (REE) scheduling and generators that failed to deliver voltage control. It ruled out a cyberattack.
   - https://www.lamoncloa.gob.es/consejodeministros/resumenes/paginas/2025/170625-rueda-de-prensa-ministros.aspx

3. **Sabotage ruled out.** The Audiencia Nacional closed its criminal case, finding not even a "minimal indication" of sabotage.
   - https://www.poderjudicial.es/cgpj/es/Poder-Judicial/Noticias-Judiciales/El-juez-de-la-Audiencia-Nacional-archiva-la-investigacion-por-el-apagon-general-del-pasado-el-28-de-abril-al-no-existir--un-minimo-indicio--de-sabotaje-terrorista

## Contested or unresolved

- **Responsibility.**
  - REE blames generators: https://www.ree.es/en/press-office/news/press-release/2025/06/red-electrica-presents-report-incident-28-april-and-proposes-recommendations
  - Aelec, the utilities' association, blames REE: https://en.ara.cat/economy/the-power-companies-attribute-the-blackout-to-poor-management-by-red-electrica_1_5421076.html
  - The regulator, CNMC, has opened sanction proceedings against REE ("very serious") and against generators. These are unresolved and do not prejudge the outcome. Reports disagree on how many proceedings there are.
  - https://www.pv-magazine.es/2026/04/21/la-cnmc-incoa-expedientes-sancionadores-por-el-apagon-a-ree-y-las-electricas-estas-ultimas-comienzan-su-comparecencia-en-el-congreso/

- **Where the oscillation came from.** REE has named Iberdrola's Núñez de Balboa PV plant; Iberdrola denies it.
  - https://www.pv-magazine.com/2025/06/19/iberdrolas-500-mw-nunez-de-balboa-pv-plant-blamed-by-ree-for-spain-blackout
  - https://files.griddo.comillas.edu/resumen-informe-preliminar-comillas-iit-rouco-lobato-echavarren-v16_1.pdf

- **Gaps the panel acknowledged.** Missing data means the panel could not explain why some units tripped or why some missed their reactive-power targets.
  - https://sciencemediacentre.es/en/final-blackout-report-european-operators-confirms-event-was-caused-multiple-factors-recommends

- **Panel impartiality.** Iberdrola has challenged it because REE sat on the panel.
  - https://www.energias-renovables.com/panorama/iberdrola-duda-de-la-imparcialidad-del-informe-20260421

## Not covered

- Portuguese reviews (REN, ERSE)
- the Spanish Senate inquiry
- any independent measurement study (PMU data) checking the official timeline

answer.text:
**Established by official investigations**

- **The mechanism.** This was an overvoltage collapse, not a frequency or inertia event. ENTSO-E's expert panel published its final report on 20 March 2026. It found "a combination of many interacting factors": oscillations, gaps in voltage and reactive-power control, differences in voltage-regulation practice, rapid output cuts and generator disconnections in Spain, and uneven stabilisation capabilities. These caused fast voltage rises and a cascade of disconnections. The panel's factual report came out on 3 October 2025. [ENTSO-E](https://www.entsoe.eu/news/2026/03/20/entso-e-publishes-expert-panel-final-report-on-28-april-2025-blackout-in-spain-and-portugal/), [report page](https://www.entsoe.eu/publications/blackout/28-april-2025-iberian-blackout/)
- **Sequence, as summarised by trade press.**
  - At 12:32:57 a transformer near Granada tripped on overvoltage (355 MW).
  - At 12:33:16, 727 MW of solar was lost near Badajoz, and 928 MW more followed.
  - In total more than 2.5 GW was lost in about 78 seconds, and synchronism with Europe was lost at 12:33:19.
  - Several synchronous generators met their reactive-power setpoint less than 75% of the time. Some generator overvoltage protection was set below the regulatory limits. Shunt reactors are switched by hand and were not reconnected in time. Spain's 400 kV voltage band is wider than its neighbours', which left little margin before generators disconnected.
  - Sources: [POWER](https://www.powermag.com/anatomy-of-a-blackout-findings-from-the-spain-portugal-grid-collapse-final-report/), [pv magazine](https://www.pv-magazine.com/2026/03/23/entso-e-report-finds-systemic-failures-behind-2025-iberian-blackout/)
- **Spanish government report (17 June 2025).** It also blamed overvoltage and a lack of voltage-control capacity, and ruled out a cyberattack. [Energía Estratégica](https://energiaestrategica.com/strategicenergy/en/notes/spanish-goverment-report-blackout)
- **CNMC (the Spanish regulator).** It agrees the origin was "multifactorial". [CNMC](https://cnmc.es/prensa/incoacion-incidente-electrico-28A-20260417)

**Still unresolved or contested**

1. **Who is to blame.**
   - The operator, REE, says "no cause attributable to Red Eléctrica" and points to generators' incorrect disconnections and weak voltage control. [Energías Renovables](https://www.energias-renovables.com/panorama/ree-no-fall--en-el-apag-20260320)
   - The utilities' association, Aelec, blames REE's voltage control and generation scheduling. [Euronews](https://es.euronews.com/2025/06/18/red-electrica-contradice-al-gobierno-y-culpa-a-las-electricas-por-el-apagon-masivo-del-28-)
2. **Pending sanctions.** In April 2026 the CNMC opened proceedings: one against REE for a "very serious" infringement and about 20 or more against generators for "serious" ones. It says these do not attribute the cause of the blackout to anyone. The REE case has up to 18 months to run. I found no rulings yet. [El Independiente](https://www.elindependiente.com/economia/2026/04/17/cnmc-investiga-red-electrica-apagon-multas-60-millones/)
3. **Gaps in the investigation.** The panel could not determine:
   - why some generators fell short on reactive power;
   - the exact role of the 0.63 Hz oscillation, which was driven by inverter-based generation in southern Spain;

# Should you stop 16:8 because of the "91% higher risk" headline?

**Short answer:** This evidence alone isn't a reason to stop. The study behind the headline is weak and didn't measure what you're doing. It also can't prove long-term safety, so ongoing monitoring is still worthwhile.

## Where the number comes from

- **The original source** was a March 2024 American Heart Association conference abstract using US survey data (NHANES), with about 20,000 adults followed for a median of 8 years. People eating within **less than** 8 hours had a 91% higher risk of cardiovascular death (HR 1.91) than those eating across 12–16 hours. It was preliminary and not peer-reviewed, and the senior author said it does not show causation. https://newsroom.heart.org/news/8-hour-time-restricted-eating-linked-to-a-91-higher-risk-of-cardiovascular-death
- **The peer-reviewed version** was published in 2025. Compared with a 12–14 hour window, it reported HR 2.35, with a wide confidence interval of 1.39–3.98. It found no link with death from all causes or from cancer, and the authors acknowledge possible residual confounding. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40849219/

## Why the evidence is weak

- **Small group:** Only 414 people (about 2%) were in the short-window group, with roughly 31 cardiovascular deaths.
- **Poor measurement:** Each person's eating window was estimated from just two 24-hour food recalls at enrollment. That is not the same as a deliberate, sustained 16:8 pattern like yours.
- **Confounding:** The short-window group had more smokers, higher BMI and more people facing higher baseline risk. Shift work and sleep weren't accounted for. A former AHA president called the result "not ready for prime-time." https://www.tctmd.com/news/intermittent-fasting-study-sparks-debate-over-increases-cv-mortality
- **Critics with a stake:** 34 time-restricted eating researchers raised similar objections. They advocate the approach, so weigh their view accordingly. https://www.nutritioninsight.com/news/scientists-dispute-study-linking-time-restricted-eating-to-poor-heart-health.html

## Counter-evidence and limits

- **Randomized trials** show neutral to modestly positive effects on weight and blood pressure. However, they are short and none measures heart attacks or deaths. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC9644535/
- **Another observational analysis** found the lowest risk at about 11–12 hour windows. It found no significant risk from short windows in younger adults after full adjustment. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC12610411/

## What I'd do in your position

1. If 16:8 is working for your weight, continuing is reasonable. Losing excess weight has well-established heart benefits.
2. Check blood pressure, lipids and glucose at your routine visits. Some trial data hint at small LDL rises.
3. If you'd rather hedge, widening your window to about 10 hours probably keeps most of the benefit. Prioritise food quality and sleep either way.

Its advice to check markers at routine visits fits the key's 'talking to a doctor is reasonable but not required.'

No, this isn't safe. In this setup WAL mode itself is unsupported, not just risky. SQLite's own documentation rules it out on three separate points.

**1. WAL does not work across machines.** WAL keeps a small index in memory that every connection must share. It does this by memory-mapping a `-shm` file next to the database, and separate hosts can't share that memory. The WAL page says: "All processes using a database must be on the same host computer; WAL does not work over a network filesystem." The only workaround is `locking_mode=EXCLUSIVE`, which allows a single process to access the database. That rules out three servers.

**2. Locking over NFS can be broken, which risks corruption.** Even in the older rollback-journal mode, SQLite depends on the filesystem's locks being correct. The corruption guide says faulty locks are "especially true of network filesystems and NFS in particular." If two processes write at the same time on broken locks, the database "might" be corrupted. The "when to use" page adds that "there is nothing SQLite can do to prevent it." The network-use page says the same: "Rely upon it at your (and your customers') peril."

**3. It's slow and against the intended design.** Every page read and write would go over the network. The SQLite docs give this rule of thumb: avoid SQLite when the same database is "accessed directly… and simultaneously from many computers over a network."

**What to do instead** (in order of preference):

- **Use a client/server database, such as PostgreSQL.** At 20 writes per second from three servers, this is the standard answer, and it's what SQLite's docs recommend.
- **Keep SQLite on one host.** Put the database on one server's local disk and run WAL there. The other two servers send their reads and writes to a small service on that host instead of opening the file.
- **Use rollback mode over NFS only if you must.** The docs say this mode reduces the network problems, but it's untested by SQLite, allows only one writer at a time, and the corruption risk is still on you. I wouldn't use it for production data.

Since a corrupted shared database could take down all three servers, I'd go with PostgreSQL.

**Sources:**
- https://www.sqlite.org/wal.html
- https://www.sqlite.org/useovernet.html
- https://www.sqlite.org/howtocorrupt.html
- https://www.sqlite.org/whentouse.html

grade.decision_why: It gives a clear 'No' for multi-host WAL over NFS. It cites SQLite's statement that WAL needs all processes on the same host with shared memory, and that NFS locking is unreliable and risks corruption. It recommends the same alternatives as the key: a client/server database, or a single host running SQLite with a service in front of it.

# No: 3.13t isn't production-ready for this service. The free-threaded target is 3.14t.

**Why not 3.13t**

- **CPython calls it experimental.** The 3.13 docs say to "expect some bugs and a substantial single-threaded performance hit," about 40% on pyperformance. They also list known crashes: shared iterators, and reading frames from another thread. Third-party measurements put the slowdown at 17–40%, depending on workload. Sources: https://docs.python.org/3.13/howto/free-threading-python.html, https://static-frame.readthedocs.io/en/latest/articles/freethread.html, https://codspeed.io/blog/state-of-python-3-13-performance-free-threading
- **PEP 779 makes 3.13 "Phase I, explicitly experimental."** 3.14t is the officially supported build, though still optional. https://peps.python.org/pep-0779/
- **The ecosystem has dropped 3.13t.**
  - cibuildwheel deprecated cp313t builds: https://github.com/pypa/cibuildwheel/pull/2787
  - manylinux removed cp313t from its images in May 2026, and PyTorch followed: https://dev-discuss.pytorch.org/t/dropping-python-3-13t-free-threaded-support-in-nightlies-and-in-the-future-pytorch-2-13-release/3386
- **Your dependencies have dropped it too.** The current NumPy 2.5.4, lxml 6.1.3 and pydantic-core 2.50.4 ship cp314t wheels but no cp313t ones. That would leave you on stale pins or source builds. The PyPI pages were truncated, so treat this as very likely rather than certain. https://pypi.org/pypi/numpy/2.5.4/json, https://pypi.org/pypi/lxml/6.1.3/json, https://pypi.org/project/pydantic-core/

**lxml is the real blocker, even on 3.14t**

- lxml's test suite segfaulted on 3.13t: https://bugs.launchpad.net/lxml/+bug/2111289
- lxml 6.x cp314t wheels re-enabled the GIL at import. We confirmed this for 6.0.2; 6.1.3 is unverified.
- Real free-threading support is only in 7.0.0a1, an alpha, for 3.14t and later: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/lxml/lxml/master/CHANGES.txt
- An unmarked extension silently turns the GIL back on, so "it installs" doesn't mean "it runs without the GIL."

**What to do**

1. **Now:** stay on standard 3.13. Get parallelism from multiprocessing, or from NumPy operations that release the GIL.
2. **Ask the platform team to allow 3.14t.** The 3.14 docs report about 1–8% single-thread overhead, against roughly 40% on 3.13t. https://docs.python.org/3.14/howto/free-threading-python.html
3. **Prototype on 3.14t.** Benchmark your own single-threaded and multi-threaded workloads against the GIL baseline.
4. **Contain lxml** until 7.x is stable: run it on one thread, behind a lock, or in a process pool.
5. **Add a guard in CI and at startup.** After all imports, assert that `sys._is_gil_enabled()` is `False`, so a silent GIL re-enable fails loudly.

The free-threading compatibility tracker is a useful way to watch dependency status: https://py-free-threading.github.io/tracking/

**Two separate slowdowns add up, and your Linux colleagues have neither.**

**1. File I/O: `node_modules` on a bind mount.** On a Mac, bind mounts pass through a file-sharing layer (VirtioFS, or the older gRPC FUSE) into Docker's Linux VM. On Linux, the container uses the host disk directly. `npm install` writes tens of thousands of small files, so this is probably the larger cost. In one Apple Silicon test, `npm install` took 4–6 s natively, 17–22 s on a full bind mount, about 7 s with `node_modules` in a named volume, and 57 s on gRPC FUSE ([sparkfabrik#61](https://github.com/sparkfabrik/sparkdock/issues/61)). A 2025 measurement found VirtioFS about 3× slower than native ([engineered.at](https://engineered.at/articles/docker-on-macos-is-still-slow)).

**2. CPU: amd64 emulation.** A `linux/amd64` image on an M3 runs under emulation, which is much slower for compile-heavy work such as native module builds and bundling ([Docker](https://docs.docker.com/build/building/multi-platform/)). Docker's settings page lists Rosetta as **off** by default, which would mean the slower QEMU emulator. Some Docker sources disagree, so check Settings → General yourself ([settings](https://docs.docker.com/desktop/settings-and-maintenance/settings/), [4.25 blog](https://www.docker.com/blog/docker-desktop-4-25/)). Docker VMM does not support Rosetta ([VMM](https://docs.docker.com/desktop/features/vmm/)).

**What to do, in order:**
1. Keep the source on a bind mount but put a **named volume over `node_modules`**, and run `npm install` inside the container ([VS Code guide](https://code.visualstudio.com/remote/advancedcontainers/improve-performance)). Confirm VirtioFS is selected.
2. Turn on **Rosetta** with the Apple Virtualization framework, not Docker VMM.
3. Best fix: **build the image as native arm64** and isolate the x86-only dependency, either in an amd64 sidecar or by finding an arm64 build. Rosetta lacks AVX and has caused hangs and 100% CPU with Vite/Next.js ([roadmap#384](https://github.com/docker/roadmap/issues/384)). Node 20 amd64 images have also hung during `npm install` ([docker-node#1946](https://www.github.com/nodejs/docker-node/issues/1946)). Check whether your x86 binary needs AVX.
4. **Upgrade off Node 20**, which reached end of life on 2026-04-30, and update Docker Desktop.
5. Optional: Synchronized File Shares (4.27+, a paid plan according to Docker's blog, which claims 2–10× gains) ([docs](https://docs.docker.com/desktop/features/synchronized-file-sharing/), [blog](https://www.docker.com/blog/announcing-synchronized-file-shares/)), or OrbStack ([vendor data](https://orbstack.dev/blog/fast-filesystem)).

**Caveat:** No source measures how much of your 5–10× comes from each cause. Time `npm install` with bind mount vs. volume, and with Rosetta on vs. off, to find out which matters most for you.

It ends with a 2x2 timing check (bind mount vs volume, Rosetta on vs off) that separates the two causes.

# Share of crates.io crates containing unsafe code: figure to cite

**Cite this:** *"About 19% of crates.io crates with significant code (24,362 of ~127,000) use the `unsafe` keyword directly, as of May 2024. A further 34.35% make a direct function call into a crate that uses `unsafe`."* The source is the Rust Foundation post "Unsafe Rust in the Wild" (21 May 2024): https://rustfoundation.org/media/unsafe-rust-in-the-wild-notes-on-the-current-state-of-unsafe-rust/. One researcher reached it under `/news/` instead of `/media/`, so check which URL is canonical before publishing.

**Corroboration:** Evans, Campbell & Soffa (ICSE 2020, peer-reviewed) is the only corroborating source we checked against the original text: https://arxiv.org/abs/2007.00752. The abstract says `unsafe` is used in "less than 30% of Rust libraries". It also says more than half of libraries "cannot be entirely statically checked" because of unsafe code in their call chain.

## Confidence

- **High** that direct use falls somewhere between about 19% and 30%. Independent studies from 2020 to 2024 agree on this range.
- **Moderate** on the exact figure. An auditor will raise these points:
  - **Arithmetic:** 24,362 / 127,000 is 19.18%, not the 19.11% the post states. Measured against all ~145,000 crates, the share would be ~16.8%. Write "≈19%" and name the denominator.
  - **Definitions:** "Significant code" is never defined.
  - **Method:** The post is not peer-reviewed. Its data comes from the Foundation's Painter tool (https://github.com/rustfoundation/painter), which only covers crates that build. Painter does not resolve callee versions and can miss calls made through generics or dynamic dispatch.
  - **Age:** The data is about 2.5 years old. We found no census from 2025 or 2026.

## How to frame it for a risk assessment

- **The 19% is a floor, not a measure of exposure.** It counts crates, not downloads, and popular crates use `unsafe` more often. Transitive exposure is above 50% according to Evans.
- **Keyword presence does not mean a vulnerability exists.** The Foundation itself says most of this unsafe code is likely not exploitable.

## Do not cite yet

- **Astrauskas et al., OOPSLA 2020** (https://doi.org/10.1145/3428204). Secondary summaries disagree, giving either ~23.6% or ~25%. None of us could open the paper itself.
- **Evans's detailed breakdowns** (29%, the share of popular crates, ~15k crates). These come only from secondary summaries.
- **The Reddit claim** that "72.5% contain no unsafe". We could not trace where it comes from.

If you obtain the Astrauskas paper, you could add a second peer-reviewed cross-check.

# Should our SQLite database live on a shared NFS mount?

**No. The plan as described is unsafe, and the WAL part cannot work at all.**

## Why WAL fails across hosts

SQLite's WAL documentation says: "All processes using a database must be on the same host computer; WAL does not work over a network filesystem." WAL coordinates writers through a shared-memory index (the `-shm` file). Processes on three different machines cannot share that memory, so this is a design limit, not something tuning can fix. The only exception is `locking_mode=EXCLUSIVE`, which allows a single process only. https://www.sqlite.org/wal.html

## Why NFS is risky even without WAL

- **SQLite advises against it.** SQLite is "not tested in across-a-network scenarios." Locks on network filesystems "have been known to operate incorrectly… This has led to database corruption." The page says to use networked access "at your (and your customers') peril." https://www.sqlite.org/useovernet.html
- **NFS is singled out for locking bugs.** SQLite names "network filesystems and NFS in particular" as a source of broken locks. https://www.sqlite.org/howtocorrupt.html
- **NFS doesn't guarantee consistency between clients.** The Linux man page says NFS "is not designed to support true cluster file system cache coherence." https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man5/nfs.5.html
- **Corruption can be silent.** NFS may report a lock as granted when it isn't. The damage then shows up later, not at the moment it happens. https://sqlite.org/forum/forumpost/02c1a784a2830a3d?raw
- **Red Hat agrees.** Its answer is "In most cases no," even with NFSv4's improved locking. https://access.redhat.com/solutions/120733

## Rollback-journal mode as a fallback

Switching to rollback-journal mode removes the WAL problem, but it is still at your own risk. Writes block all readers, and every lock and fsync becomes a network round trip. In one test on AWS EFS (NFSv4), 39 of 50 concurrent writes failed with "database is locked." https://zenn.dev/galette/articles/sqlite-on-efs-locking

At 20 writes/s from three hosts, expect frequent `SQLITE_BUSY` errors. A short test without corruption also proves little, because these failures are rare and hard to reproduce.

## What to do instead

1. **Use PostgreSQL (or MySQL).** This is the standard answer for several app servers sharing one database, and SQLite's own docs recommend it: https://www.sqlite.org/whentouse.html
2. **Keep SQLite on local disk on one host.** That host runs WAL and serves reads and writes to the other two through a small service. This is SQLite's own "proxy" suggestion (useovernet link above).
3. **Try a replication layer** such as rqlite or LiteFS. These are worth evaluating, but our research didn't cover them.

At your load, option 1 is the simplest robust choice. Option 2 works if you want to keep SQLite.

It grounds this in SQLite's WAL docs (WAL needs shared memory on one host and does not work over a network filesystem) and in NFS locking unreliability and corruption risk. It recommends the alternatives the key lists: a client/server DB, a single-host proxy or writer service in front of SQLite, and a replication layer. This matches the key's decision and actions.

- https://www.sqlite.org/useovernet.html

- **It's untested and not recommended.** SQLite isn't tested over networks. The SQLite docs warn that lock bugs on NFS have corrupted databases, sometimes silently and much later. Red Hat's answer to running SQLite on NFS is "in most cases no", even for NFSv4.
  - https://www.sqlite.org/howtocorrupt.html
  - https://www.sqlite.org/whentouse.html
  - https://access.redhat.com/solutions/120733

  - https://zenn.dev/galette/articles/sqlite-on-efs-locking
  - https://lambrospetrou-github-io.vercel.app/articles/aws-lambda-and-sqlite-over-efs

SQLite's own guidance for a site busy enough to need several servers is to use a client/server database. About 20 writes per second is easy for PostgreSQL, or for SQLite on local disk behind a single owner host.

# Iberian blackout, 28 April 2025: cause and open disputes

**Caveat:** None of the researchers read the ENTSO-E final report PDF. The findings below come from its landing page and press summaries. Check the wording against the PDF before quoting it. The summaries disagree on details such as the page count (440–472) and the number of recommendations (21 or 22).

## Official findings

**ENTSO-E Expert Panel, final report (20 March 2026).** The panel found no single cause, and says the report is "not an attribution of liability." The interacting factors were:
- oscillations: a 0.63 Hz forced oscillation from converter-based generation and a 0.2 Hz inter-area mode, which set conditions but were not the direct trigger;
- gaps in voltage and reactive-power control;
- divergent voltage-regulation practices;
- rapid output cuts and generator disconnections in Spain.

Together these caused a fast overvoltage and cascading generation trips from about 12:32–12:33 CEST, followed by loss of synchronism.

Contributing details reported:
- Synchronous units missed reactive setpoints, with no penalty for doing so.
- Renewables ran at fixed power factor.
- Shunt reactors were switched by hand.
- Spain allows a wide voltage band (up to 435 kV).
- Protection settings were misaligned.
- Some trips remain unexplained because fault records are missing.

Sources: https://www.entsoe.eu/publications/blackout/28-april-2025-iberian-blackout/ · https://www.powermag.com/anatomy-of-a-blackout-findings-from-the-spain-portugal-grid-collapse-final-report/

**ENTSO-E factual report (3 October 2025).** It sets out the timeline only, with no root-cause analysis. https://www.pv-tech.org/over-voltage-triggered-iberian-blackout-report/

**Spanish Government committee (17 June 2025).** It named three causes:
- insufficient voltage control (REE scheduled 10 synchronous units, one became unavailable, and some did not respond properly);
- oscillations;
- apparently improper disconnections.

It ruled out a cyberattack. https://www.lamoncloa.gob.es/consejodeministros/resumenes/Documents/2025/Informe-no-confidencial-Comite-de-analisis-28A.pdf

**Audiencia Nacional (12 January 2026).** The court closed the sabotage case for lack of evidence. https://www.elindependiente.com/espana/2026/01/12/el-juez-archiva-la-investigacion-por-el-apagon-al-no-existir-un-minimo-indicio-de-sabotaje/

**CNMC (2026).** It made recommendations and opened sanction proceedings. The CNMC states these proceedings do not assign cause. Reports put the number at about 20 or up to 64, and no rulings were found. https://www.cnmc.es/prensa/informe-incidente-electrico-20260319

## Contested (mark as such)

- **Who is responsible.**
  - REE blames generators: https://www.ree.es/sites/default/files/2025-06/NP_RedElectrica_InformeOS_180625.pdf
  - Aelec, Endesa and Iberdrola blame REE's scheduling: https://en.ara.cat/economy/the-power-companies-attribute-the-blackout-to-poor-management-by-red-electrica_1_5421076.html
  - REE's claim that ENTSO-E clears it is REE's own reading: https://www.ree.es/sites/default/files/2026-03/NP%20-%20FinalReport%20Expert%20Panel%2020%20marzo.pdf
- **Whether the 0.6 Hz oscillation was forced, and where it came from.** REE named Iberdrola's Núñez de Balboa PV plant, which Iberdrola denies. An industry-commissioned Comillas-IIT study calls it an inter-area mode. https://www.pv-magazine.com/2025/06/19/iberdrolas-500-mw-nunez-de-balboa-pv-plant-blamed-by-ree-for-spain-blackout · https://files.griddo.comillas.edu/resumen-informe-preliminar-comillas-iit-rouco-lobato-echavarren-v16_1.pdf
- **Senate report (April 2026).** It blames REE, the government and the CNMC. It is a political document. https://www.vozpopuli.com/economia/energia/el-senado-senala-como-culpables-del-apagon-a-red-electrica-el-gobierno-y-la-cnmc-.html
- **Unresolved in the official findings.** Why units missed their setpoints, unexplained trips, and missing data for small and distributed generation.

No independent (non-industry) re-analysis of the PMU data was found.

I found that the official investigations agree on the mechanism: overvoltage leading to a cascade. They don't agree on who is responsible, and no official investigation assigns blame. A caveat on sourcing: I couldn't read the ENTSO-E final report (the PDF is over the fetch size limit) or the Spanish government's report directly. Their findings below come from ENTSO-E's summary page and from trade press. Check figures and quotes against the PDFs before you cite them.

**Established cause (supported by every official report)**
- **No single cause.** The ENTSO-E expert panel's final report (20 March 2026) names many interacting factors. These include oscillations at 0.63 Hz and 0.2 Hz, gaps in voltage and reactive power control, differing voltage regulation practices, fast output cuts and generator disconnections in Spain, and uneven ability to damp oscillations. Together they caused a rapid voltage rise and cascading generation trips. Spain and Portugal lost synchronism with Europe at 12:33:19.
- **Specific findings reported from the ENTSO-E report:** several conventional units missed their reactive power setpoints; shunt reactors were switched by hand, which was too slow; renewables ran at a fixed power factor; some plants tripped below the regulatory voltage limits; and small rooftop solar disconnected. Lack of inertia was not a root cause.
- **Spanish government committee (17 June 2025):** overvoltage with several causes. Red Eléctrica (REE) did not schedule enough voltage-control generation the day before. Synchronous plants absorbed less reactive power than expected. Some disconnections were "apparently improper."
- **Ruled out:** a cyberattack, by the government report and by the National Court (Audiencia Nacional), which provisionally closed its case.
- **CNMC, the Spanish regulator (19 March 2026):** the tools and obligations to prevent the blackout already existed.

**Still contested**
- **Who is responsible.** REE says the ENTSO-E report finds no cause attributable to it, and blames generators: missed voltage-control obligations (operating procedure P.O. 7.4) and at least nine incorrect disconnections. The utilities' association Aelec (Iberdrola, Endesa, EDP) says "La operativa fue la que falló" ("it was the operation that failed"), and Iberdrola has sued REE for defamation. ENTSO-E and the CNMC both say they are not assigning liability.

The CNMC says opening them does not attribute the cause of the blackout. I haven't confirmed any outcomes after April 2026.
- **Gaps in the evidence:** the role of the oscillations is unclear, and missing data left the cause of some disconnections undetermined.
- **Role of renewables:** ENTSO-E's president said the problem was voltage control, not renewables. How much renewables contributed is still debated.

2. **`--platform linux/amd64` emulates all of Node**, not just the x86-only dependency. QEMU is much slower than native: https://docs.docker.com/build/building/multi-platform/

   - Rosetta also has known bugs, including missing AVX support: https://github.com/docker/roadmap/issues/384

**Decision: No. Don't put the SQLite database on the shared NFS mount for all three servers, in WAL mode or any other mode.** Use one of these instead:

- **PostgreSQL or MySQL.** This is SQLite's own first recommendation when several machines need to write. https://www.sqlite.org/useovernet.html, https://www.sqlite.org/whentouse.html
- **One server owns the SQLite file** on its local disk, in WAL mode, and the other two send reads and writes to it through an API. 20 writes/s is easy for SQLite on a single host; the problem is the layout, not the load.
- **A tool built for shared SQLite**, such as LiteFS or rqlite. None of the researchers evaluated these.

**Rests on:** WAL keeps its coordination index in a memory-mapped `-shm` file, and processes on different machines cannot share that memory. SQLite's documentation says: "All processes using a database must be on the same host computer; WAL does not work over a network filesystem." https://www.sqlite.org/wal.html. Richard Hipp, SQLite's author, says a cross-host WAL setup that seems to work "just means you didn't test it enough." https://mail-archive.com/sqlite-users@mailinglists.sqlite.org/msg108685.html. OpenAI's Codex documentation reports this exact failure: Linux hosts opening one WAL database over NFS corrupted it. Two researchers gave slightly different URLs for that page; this is one of them: https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/environments/network-file-systems. NFS version doesn't change any of this, because the problem is shared memory, not locking.

Switching to rollback-journal mode doesn't make it safe either. SQLite doesn't test it over a network, failures are rare and hard to reproduce, and NFS locking is a named cause of corruption. https://www.sqlite.org/howtocorrupt.html, https://www.sqlite.org/faq.html (Q5)

**Not verified:** Nothing that would change the decision. No one tested your NFSv4 server or mount options, and no published benchmark of rollback mode on NFSv4 exists. Those would only matter if you wanted to try rollback mode, which I advise against.

**Next check:** None needed for this decision. Separately, one report says the corruption page describes a "WAL-reset bug" affecting SQLite 3.7.0 through 3.51.2, even on a single host. If you go with the single-owner option, check your SQLite version against https://www.sqlite.org/howtocorrupt.html.

**Decision:** Two stacked causes are likely: file I/O on the bind-mounted `node_modules`, and x86 emulation of the whole image. Fix the first now. Run one timing test before restructuring for the second.

1. **Do now:** keep the source bind-mounted, but put `node_modules` on a named volume and run `npm install` inside the container. VS Code documents this setup for devcontainers. In an independent test on an M4 Pro, `npm install` took 9.53s on a bind mount, 3.61s with a named volume and 3.37s on the host:
   - https://code.visualstudio.com/remote/advancedcontainers/improve-performance
   - https://www.paolomainardi.com/posts/docker-performance-macos-2025/
2. **Check settings:** in Docker Desktop, set file sharing to VirtioFS (https://docs.docker.com/desktop/settings-and-maintenance/settings/). Also look at "Use Rosetta for x86_64/amd64 emulation", which needs the Apple Virtualization framework VMM (https://docs.docker.com/desktop/features/vmm/). Sources disagree on whether Rosetta is on by default, so look at your machine. Without Rosetta, Docker falls back to QEMU, which is much slower (https://docs.docker.com/build/building/multi-platform/). Rosetta has known cases of Node builds hanging or pinning a CPU:
   - https://github.com/docker/roadmap/issues/384
   - https://github.com/nodejs/docker-node/issues/1946
3. **Dev server:** remove `CHOKIDAR_USEPOLLING` or `WATCHPACK_POLLING` if either is set, because polling a bind mount wastes CPU (https://github.com/docker/for-mac/issues/7274).
4. **Likely next step:** build the image as native arm64 and run only the x86-only dependency as a separate amd64 service. Also check whether that dependency now has an arm64 build.

```text
Decision: Named volume for node_modules now; time arm64 vs amd64 before restructuring the image.
Rests on: An independent benchmark (Mainardi, M4 Pro, Docker Desktop 4.37) measured a ~2.8× bind-mount penalty for npm install that a named volume removes. Your amd64 image is emulated on an M3 by construction; the size of that penalty comes only from sysbench runs and anecdotes, 1.2–6× (https://vpsmac.com/en/blog/docker-on-m4-mac-linux-container-performance-analysis.html, https://github.com/orbstack/orbstack/issues/2744).
Not verified: How much of your 5–10× is emulation versus I/O. Whether your Docker uses Rosetta or QEMU. An unconfirmed report that amd64/Rosetta got slower on macOS 27 (orbstack #2744).
Next check: With node_modules on a named volume, time `npm ci` in an arm64 container and in your amd64 one. A large gap means the arm64 split is worth doing.
```

If your plan is paid, Docker's Synchronized file shares are another option (https://docs.docker.com/desktop/features/synchronized-file-sharing/). Its "2–10× faster" figure is Docker's own marketing number, and the independent test above found it no faster than a named volume.

**Decision:** Don't run the service on 3.13t. Keep standard 3.13 and use multiprocessing for the CPU-bound work. If free-threading matters to you, ask your platform team to allow 3.14 and pilot 3.14t. Don't commit to 3.14t in production until it passes on your own workload.

**Why 3.13t is ruled out**
- CPython calls 3.13t experimental. Its docs warn of "some bugs and a substantial single-threaded performance hit" of about 40%, and they list ways to crash it. https://docs.python.org/3.13/howto/free-threading-python.html
- PEP 779 keeps 3.13 at the experimental stage. Free-threading becomes "supported but optional" only in 3.14. https://peps.python.org/pep-0779/ The 3.14 release notes put the single-thread penalty at about 5–10%. https://docs.python.org/3.14/whatsnew/3.14.html
- pypa/manylinux removed cp313t from its build images on 2026-05-07, and PyTorch dropped 3.13t wheels as a result. https://dev-discuss.pytorch.org/t/dropping-python-3-13t-free-threaded-support-in-nightlies-and-in-the-future-pytorch-2-13-release/3386
- The researchers read the PyPI file lists for the latest releases of all three of your dependencies. NumPy 2.5.4, pydantic-core 2.50.4 and lxml 6.1.3 each ship cp314t x86-64 wheels and none ship cp313t. https://pypi.org/project/numpy/#files, https://pypi.org/project/pydantic-core/#files, https://pypi.org/project/lxml/#files
  - Some older releases did ship cp313t wheels, for example pydantic-core from 2.29.0. https://newreleases.io/project/pypi/pydantic-core/release/2.29.0
  - Pinning to those releases would leave you without security fixes. That matters most for lxml, which parses untrusted XML.

**Risks that remain on 3.14t**
- Free-threading support is still labelled experimental in all three libraries:
  - NumPy: https://numpy.org/devdocs/reference/thread_safety.html
  - pydantic: https://pydantic.dev/articles/pydantic-v2-11-release
  - lxml 7.0.0a1: https://pypi.org/project/lxml/7.0.0a1/
- NumPy arrays shared between threads need your own locking.
- lxml has published nothing on thread safety under free-threading.
- If any extension you import isn't marked free-thread-safe, the GIL silently turns back on. https://pyo3.rs/v0.23.2/free-threading

```text
Decision: Don't deploy 3.13t; stay on standard 3.13 + multiprocessing; pilot 3.14t.
Rests on: CPython docs/PEP 779 (3.13t experimental) and the current PyPI file lists of
          NumPy, pydantic-core and lxml showing cp314t wheels only, read by the researchers.
Not verified: Whether 3.14t keeps the GIL off and runs faster for your service, and whether
          lxml/NumPy stay stable under your threading pattern. Nobody has run your workload.
Next check: In a 3.14t environment, install your full dependency set, import it, and confirm
          sys._is_gil_enabled() is False. Then benchmark single-threaded and at N threads
          against GIL 3.14, measuring memory too.
```

Third-party benchmarks for 3.13t vary (17–40% slower single-threaded), but none of them would change this decision. https://codspeed.io/blog/state-of-python-3-13-performance-free-threading

It also makes the 3.14t move conditional on checking free-threaded wheels for every dependency and testing on the real workload, which is the key's 'after confirming free-threaded wheels' condition.

**Decision: cite "about 19% of crates.io crates directly contain `unsafe` (Rust Foundation, May 2024)" as the headline figure, with Cui et al.'s 20.8% (January 2023 snapshot) as independent corroboration.** You can state "roughly one in five" with confidence. Do not claim precision beyond that.

**Primary source.** All three researchers read the Rust Foundation post, "Unsafe Rust in the Wild" (21 May 2024): https://rustfoundation.org/media/unsafe-rust-in-the-wild-notes-on-the-current-state-of-unsafe-rust/ (one researcher reached it at a `/news/` path; check which URL resolves before you publish). It reports 24,362 of about 127,000 crates "with significant code" (19.11%), measured with the Painter tool: https://github.com/rustfoundation/painter. For supply-chain exposure, the same post gives a better-suited figure: another 34.35% of crates directly call into a crate that uses `unsafe`.

**Corroboration.** Two researchers read this in the primary text: "21,506 crates use Unsafe Rust among the 103,516 crates on crates.io (3,614 are yanked)", snapshot 2023-01-30, which is 20.8%. It was published by Cui et al. at ICSE 2024: https://arxiv.org/html/2308.04785. A related preprint by the same group repeats the count: https://arxiv.org/html/2412.06251v1. Treat these as one data point, not two. Their method (regex over source) differs from the Foundation's, so the two figures agree only roughly.

**Caveats auditors will raise**
- 24,362 ÷ 127,000 = 19.18%, not 19.11%, so the published denominator is rounded.
- "Significant code" is never defined. About 18,000 of about 145,000 crates were excluded.
- No dataset is published, so the figure can be traced but not reproduced.
- The data is 2.5 years old. No researcher found a 2025–2026 registry-wide census.
- Using `unsafe` is not the same as being vulnerable. Much of it is FFI or SIMD.

**Do not cite yet:** the 2020 figures (Astrauskas et al. ~25%, Evans et al. ~29%, and ">50% of popular crates"). No researcher could open those PDFs, so these numbers come only from secondary summaries. An auditor checking them could find a mismatch.

```text
Decision: Cite ~19% (Rust Foundation, May 2024; 24,362 of ~127,000 crates), corroborated by 20.8% (Cui et al., Jan 2023); add 34.35% for direct dependency exposure.
Rests on: Both figures read in their primary sources by the researchers.
Not verified: The Foundation's exact denominator and definition; any post-2024 change; the 2020 percentages (secondary only).
Next check: None needed for the headline. Read the Astrauskas and Evans PDFs only if you want a trend line.
```

That overstates how settled a 2024 snapshot is for today's crates.io, even though the answer elsewhere lists post-2024 change as unverified.

- **The ecosystem has dropped 3.13t.** manylinux removed it from its build images on 2026-05-07, and PyTorch followed. **Decision: No. Do not put the SQLite database on the shared NFS mount for all three servers to write. Use PostgreSQL, or keep the SQLite file on local disk on one host and have the other two servers send their reads and writes to a service on that host.**

**Rests on:** WAL mode cannot work across machines. This is a limit of how WAL is built, not a tuning issue. WAL coordinates through a shared-memory index (the `-shm` file), and processes on different hosts cannot share memory. SQLite's docs say: "All processes using a database must be on the same host computer; WAL does not work over a network filesystem" (https://www.sqlite.org/wal.html). Two researchers read this page directly. Because the limit comes from the design, it applies to your three servers without anyone needing to test it on your setup. The same docs recommend the two alternatives above (https://www.sqlite.org/useovernet.html).

**Why rollback-journal mode isn't a good fallback:**
- **Corruption risk depends on NFS locking.** SQLite says locking bugs are "especially true of network filesystems and NFS in particular" and lead to corruption (https://www.sqlite.org/howtocorrupt.html). It also says it is "not tested in across-a-network scenarios" and warns that early test success proves little, because failures are infrequent and hard to reproduce (https://www.sqlite.org/useovernet.html).
- **NFS doesn't promise coherence.** NFS "is not designed to support true cluster file system cache coherence" (https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man5/nfs.5.html). Red Hat's answer for SQLite on NFS is "In most cases no," even for v4 (https://access.redhat.com/solutions/120733).
- **Expect poor performance at your load.** Rollback mode blocks readers during every write, and each lock and sync is a network round trip. In one EFS (NFSv4) test, 39 of 50 concurrent writes failed with "database is locked" (https://zenn.dev/galette/articles/sqlite-on-efs-locking). Another measured about 140 ms per transaction, compared with 30–40 ms on local disk (https://lambrospetrou-github-io.vercel.app/articles/aws-lambda-and-sqlite-over-efs).
- **SQLite's own guidance fits your case.** If a site "requires multiple servers," use a client/server database (https://www.sqlite.org/whentouse.html).

**Not verified:** Nobody tested rollback mode against your NFS server and mount options. That gap doesn't affect the decision, because the WAL plan fails by design and the fallback is risky and slow either way.

**Next check:** None needed. If you'd rather keep SQLite than move to PostgreSQL, the next step is to evaluate replication layers such as rqlite or LiteFS. None of the researchers covered those.

grade.decision_why: The final answer says no to multi-host SQLite over NFS. It grounds this in SQLite's own WAL documentation: shared memory means all processes must be on the same host. It recommends a client-server database (PostgreSQL) or a single-host service in front of SQLite, and mentions replication layers (rqlite/LiteFS) as an option. This matches the key's decision and its alternatives.

  - NumPy 2.5.4 and lxml 6.1.3 ship cp314t wheels but no cp313t ones. https://pypi.org/pypi/numpy/2.5.4/json, https://pypi.org/pypi/lxml/6.1.3/json
  - pydantic-core 2.50.4 also has no cp313t wheels, though that page was truncated when read. https://pypi.org/project/pydantic-core/
- **lxml has no free-threading support on 3.13t at all.** Its support is "enabled in Python 3.14t and later", and only from the 7.0.0a1 alpha. Older lxml re-enabled the GIL on import, and its tests segfaulted under 3.13t. So even pinning old wheels would bring the GIL back. https://raw.githubusercontent.com/lxml/lxml/master/CHANGES.txt, https://bugs.launchpad.net/lxml/+bug/2111289
- **The ecosystem is abandoning 3.13t.** manylinux removed it, cibuildwheel deprecated it, and PyTorch dropped it. https://github.com/pypa/cibuildwheel/pull/2787, https://dev-discuss.pytorch.org/t/dropping-python-3-13t-free-threaded-support-in-nightlies-and-in-the-future-pytorch-2-13-release/3386

**Not verified:**
- Nobody has measured your service on 3.14t. Published overhead is about 1–8% there, and third-party 3.13t numbers vary from 17% to 40%. https://docs.python.org/3.14/howto/free-threading-python.html, https://static-frame.readthedocs.io/en/latest/articles/freethread.html
- It's unknown whether lxml 6.1.3's cp314t wheels keep the GIL off.

Neither gap changes the "no 3.13t" decision. Both decide whether 3.14t is worth it.

**Next check:** On a 3.14t branch, install your dependencies and assert `sys._is_gil_enabled()` is `False` after all imports. Then benchmark single- and multi-threaded throughput against your current 3.13 GIL baseline. If lxml re-enables the GIL, confine parsing to a single thread or a process pool.

It recommends staying on the GIL build with multiprocessing. It says to move to 3.14t only after checking dependency wheels and free-threading status, and it names lxml's stable free-threaded release as the gating condition.

**Decision:** Cite **"19.1% of the ~127,000 crates on crates.io with significant code use the `unsafe` keyword directly (24,362 crates; Rust Foundation, May 2024)."** Next to it, cite the supply-chain figure from the same post: **34.35% of crates make a direct function call into another crate that uses `unsafe`.** As a peer-reviewed cross-check, cite only what the Evans et al. abstract states: `unsafe` appears in "less than 30% of Rust libraries", and "more than half" cannot be fully statically checked because of `unsafe` in their dependencies (2020).

**Rests on:** All three researchers read the Rust Foundation post directly and got the same figures from it. Auditors can trace every number in this wording to the post or to the Evans abstract.

- Rust Foundation post: https://rustfoundation.org/media/unsafe-rust-in-the-wild-notes-on-the-current-state-of-unsafe-rust/ (one researcher reached it under `/news/` instead of `/media/`)
- Evans et al. abstract: https://arxiv.org/abs/2007.00752

**Footnote the caveats an auditor will raise:**

- **The denominator isn't exact.** The post calls 19.11% a share of "all crates", but it only matches the ~127k crates with significant code. Against all ~145k crates it would be ~16.8%. Also, 24,362/127,000 is 19.18%, so the 127k figure is rounded. Write "≈19%" or "19.1% of crates with significant code", not "of all crates".
- **"Significant code" is never defined.**
- **The method isn't documented.** The data comes from the Foundation's Painter tool (https://github.com/rustfoundation/painter). It only counts crates that build, and it can miss calls.
- **The source is a blog post, not peer-reviewed.** It is also now 2.5 years old.
- **The figure counts crates equally.** It isn't weighted by downloads, so the share in a real dependency tree is probably higher.

**Confidence:** High that the quote is accurate and traceable. Moderate that it reflects today's true share.

**Not verified:**

- Nobody has checked how Painter detects `unsafe`, and no researcher found a 2025–26 census.
- The Astrauskas OOPSLA 2020 figure (~25%) and the Evans full-text breakdowns (29%, ~60% of popular crates) were only seen in secondary summaries. Don't cite them unless someone reads the papers themselves.
- Leave out the Reddit "72.5% / 94.6%" figures and the "29% → 23.6%" trend. Neither could be traced to a source.
- None of these would change which figure to cite.

**Next check:** None needed to cite the figure. If you want something newer than May 2024, the one unexplored lead is an October 2025 analysis of crates.io (https://00f.net/2025/10/17/state-of-the-rust-ecosystem/). No one opened it, and its search snippet didn't mention `unsafe`.

grade.decision_why: The answer gives the figure with its definition ('19.1% of the ~127,000 crates ... with significant code'), its source and its snapshot date (May 2024). It keeps the 34.35% direct-call figure separate and adds Evans' 'less than 30%' as a cross-check. It also gives only moderate confidence that the figure reflects today's share, which matches the key's point that no current figure is verified. The gap: it never says outright that independent studies differ by definition, landing at roughly a quarter to a third in 2020 against 19% in 2024. Evans is framed as a 'cross-check' rather than a divergent measurement, and Astrauskas is set aside as unverified.

transitive dependence on crates with unsafe
different crate populations (all vs significant/downloaded)

answer.text:
**Cause:** Two stacked slowdowns that your Linux colleagues don't have:

1. `node_modules` on a macOS bind mount, which crosses the slow file-sharing layer into Docker's VM.
2. CPU emulation of the amd64 image on your arm64 Mac.

The research found no measurement of how the 5–10× splits between them, and none was taken on your machine.

```text
Decision: Split. Make the cheap, reversible fixes now. Hold the arm64
  re-architecture until you've timed the result.
  Now:
  1. Keep the source on the bind mount, but put a named volume over
     /app/node_modules and run npm install inside the container.
     If the container runs as a non-root user, add chown in
     postCreateCommand.
  2. In Settings → General, confirm VirtioFS file sharing and
     "Use Rosetta for x86_64/amd64 emulation" with the Apple
     Virtualization framework. Not Docker VMM: it has no Rosetta
     support, so it falls back to slow emulation.
  3. Update Docker Desktop, and move from node:20 (end of life since
     April 2026) to node:22. Both fixed npm-install hangs under amd64
     emulation.
  Later, if still slow: build arm64 by default and isolate the
  x86-only dependency in an amd64 sidecar.
Rests on: File I/O: one Apple Silicon test measured npm install at
  17–22 s with a bind mount, ~7 s with a named volume and 4–6 s
  natively. Emulation: Docker's docs say amd64 on arm64 needs
  emulation and that QEMU can be much slower than native. All
  observed elsewhere, not on your Mac.
Not verified: Whether your install is on QEMU or Rosetta (Docker's
  pages disagree on the default). Whether your x86 dependency needs
  AVX, which Rosetta doesn't support. If it does, Rosetta fails and
  the arm64 split becomes necessary.
Next check: After step 1, time npm install and dev-server startup
  with Rosetta on and with it off. If it's still more than ~2× slower
  than Linux, or the x86 binary breaks under Rosetta, do the arm64
  split.
```

**Optional:** Synchronized file shares are a further option, though Docker's blog says they need a paid plan.

**Sources**
- https://github.com/sparkfabrik/sparkdock/issues/61
- https://code.visualstudio.com/remote/advancedcontainers/improve-performance
- https://docs.docker.com/build/building/multi-platform/
- https://docs.docker.com/desktop/settings-and-maintenance/settings/
- https://www.docker.com/blog/docker-desktop-4-25/
- https://docs.docker.com/desktop/features/vmm/
- https://github.com/docker/roadmap/issues/384
- https://www.github.com/nodejs/docker-node/issues/1946
- https://www.docker.com/blog/announcing-synchronized-file-shares/

grade.decision_why: The answer identifies both key causes: node_modules on a macOS bind mount, and amd64 emulation on Apple Silicon. It gives fixes for each: a named volume for node_modules, VirtioFS, and Rosetta with the Apple Virtualization framework rather than Docker VMM, with an arm64 image plus an isolated x86 dependency as the follow-up. It also proposes a check that separates the two causes: time npm install and dev-server startup with Rosetta on and off after the volume fix. Synchronized file shares are mentioned as an option. This matches the key.
grade.E3_evidence: "Update Docker Desktop, and move from node:20 (end of life since April 2026) to node:22. Both fixed npm-install hangs under amd64 emulation." This is stated as settled and acted on, but its only support is user workaround reports in a GitHub issue thread (nodejs/docker-node#1946), which one lane described as 'reportedly fixed'. The sparkdock arm64 benchmark, by contrast, is correctly flagged as 'observed elsewhere, not on your Mac'.
rivals_in_answer: amd64 emulation on Apple Silicon
bind-mount file sharing overhead (node_modules)
rivals_in_lanes: amd64 emulation on Apple Silicon
bind-mount file sharing overhead (node_modules)

**Decision:** Split. You can state the headline causal finding in the brief now. Hold every specific figure and quotation until it has been checked against the primary PDFs, because no researcher read them.

**Attributable now (official)**
- **ENTSO-E Expert Panel, final report (20 Mar 2026).** It finds no single cause. Oscillations, gaps in voltage and reactive-power control, differing voltage-regulation practices, rapid output cuts and generator disconnections in Spain, and uneven stabilising capability interacted. Together they produced a fast voltage rise and cascading generation trips from 12:33 CEST. Source: ENTSO-E's own landing page, https://www.entsoe.eu/publications/blackout/28-april-2025-iberian-blackout/
- **Spanish Government committee (17 Jun 2025).** It found a multifactor overvoltage cascade with three causes: too little voltage control, oscillations, and some disconnections outside protocol. It ruled out a cyberattack. https://www.miteco.gob.es/fr/prensa/ultimas-noticias/2025/junio/se-presenta-el-informe-del-comite-de-analisis-de-la-crisis-elect.html
- **Audiencia Nacional (12 Jan 2026).** It closed the sabotage case, per press reports. https://www.elindependiente.com/espana/2026/01/12/el-juez-archiva-la-investigacion-por-el-apagon-al-no-existir-un-minimo-indicio-de-sabotaje/
- **CNMC (Apr 2026).** It opened sanction proceedings and says these do not assign cause. https://www.cnmc.es/prensa/informe-incidente-electrico-20260319

**Mark as contested**
- **Responsibility.** REE blames generators that did not absorb reactive power: https://www.ree.es/sites/default/files/2025-06/NP_RedElectrica_InformeOS_180625.pdf. Aelec blames REE's scheduling and voltage management: https://en.ara.cat/economy/the-power-companies-attribute-the-blackout-to-poor-management-by-red-electrica_1_5421076.html
- **The oscillation.** ENTSO-E calls the 0.63 Hz oscillation forced and converter-driven (per summaries). A Comillas-IIT study commissioned by Endesa and Iberdrola calls it inter-area: https://files.griddo.comillas.edu/resumen-informe-preliminar-comillas-iit-rouco-lobato-echavarren-v16_1.pdf. The source plant (Núñez de Balboa) is alleged but unproven.
- **Unexplained trips.** ENTSO-E itself lacked fault records for some trips: https://www.heise.de/en/news/Blackout-on-the-Iberian-Peninsula-ENTSO-E-presents-final-report-11224775.html

```text
Decision: Use the multifactor overvoltage-cascade finding as the official cause; mark responsibility and the oscillation's origin as contested.
Rests on: ENTSO-E's landing-page summary and the MITECO release; all three researchers report the same framing. Everything more specific is from secondary summaries.
Not verified: the 0.63 Hz and "<75% setpoint compliance" figures, the 10 scheduled voltage-control units, the number of recommendations (21 vs 22), the number of CNMC cases (~20 vs 64), and any CNMC rulings after May 2026.
Next check: Read the executive summary of the ENTSO-E final report PDF and the Government's non-confidential report (https://www.lamoncloa.gob.es/consejodeministros/resumenes/Documents/2025/Informe-no-confidencial-Comite-de-analisis-28A.pdf) before quoting any figure.
```

It takes the official finding as a multifactor overvoltage cascade with insufficient voltage control, oscillations and generator disconnections. It says a cyberattack was ruled out. It marks responsibility between REE's scheduling and generators that missed their voltage-control duties as contested. The gap is that it drops the contested role of renewables and inertia, which the key lists and Report 1 raised.

generators failing to provide required voltage control
